description: 整个 Agent Loop。方向不只是 Tool / Planning / Memory / Multi-agent。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  For an LLM Engineer target, this is the column worth digging into the most. Agent evaluation lives in [Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/agent-eval); MCP / Harness live in [AI-Native](/docs/ai-native).

  > If the flow is highly deterministic, use a workflow. Don't build an agent for the sake of it.

    <Card title="Tool Calling" description="Schema, selection, validation, execution, timeouts, idempotency." href="/docs/agent/tool-calling" />

    <Card title="ReAct" description="Thought → Action → Observation. Don't stop at the buzzword." href="/docs/agent/react" />

    <Card title="Workflow vs Agent" description="A frequent judgment call. When not to use an agent." href="/docs/agent/workflow-vs-agent" />

    <Card title="Security" description="Injection, exfiltration, excessive agency, sandboxing." href="/docs/agent/security" />
  </CardGrid>

  ## Plan for this column

  1. Explain the loop and workflow vs agent first, with a counterexample from my own work
  2. Tie tool calling to Tariff / Gemini function calling

title: Agent Loop
description: Observe → Reason → Act。必须理解为什么需要 loop。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Defining an agent starts with the loop, not with a framework name.

  ## Must know

  You must be able to draw and explain this loop.

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Observe
 ↓
Reason
 ↓
Act
 ↓
Observe
 ↓
Reason
 ↓
Act
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  An agent runs in a loop inside an environment: observe the state, decide, act, then look at the result.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Without the loop, it's just a single LLM call. Tool results, retrieved content, and code output all have to flow back to the model so it can correct itself and keep going.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  The loop brings infinite loops, cost, and latency with it, so you need max iterations, timeouts, and budgets. Classic question: "Your agent occasionally loops for 20 steps and costs $0.50 per request. How do you debug and fix it?"

  ## Interview questions

  1. What is an agent?
  2. Explain the agent loop.
  3. Why do you need an agent loop instead of generating everything in one pass?
  4. How do you detect that the loop is spinning without making progress?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: Memory
description: 不只 short / long-term。五种 memory 各自解决什么问题。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  What memory really solves: consistency across turns, personalization, and reusing skills — not "storing the chat log."

  ## Must know

  * Conversation Memory
  * Working Memory
  * Episodic Memory
  * Semantic Memory
  * Procedural Memory
  * External Memory

  ## Mechanism

  ```
  Conversation  the current conversation
  Working       scratchpad for the current task
  Episodic      events that happened
  Semantic      stable facts / preferences
  Procedural    how to do things (skills, playbooks)
  External      files, databases, retrieval
  ```

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Memory is state that has to stay usable across steps and sessions. It isn't the same as stuffing all history into the prompt.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Working memory holds the current plan; episodic memory is retrievable; semantic memory holds user and company facts; procedural memory is how to use tools. External memory is RAG or files.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Careless writes cause context pollution and wrong personalization. Filter before writing and retrieve when reading — don't treat memory as an append-only log.

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you manage agent memory?
  2. What problem does memory actually solve?
  3. Why isn't conversation history enough?
  4. How do you correct a memory that was written wrong?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: Multi-Agent
description: supervisor / router / specialist。重点：为什么有时候反而更差。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Tie it to Supervisor → Expert in the Tariff project. Be able to argue both for splitting and for not splitting.

  ## Must know

  * supervisor
  * router
  * specialist agents
  * parallel / sequential / hierarchical agents

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Router / Supervisor
        ↓
   specialist A / B / C
```

<Locale lang="en">
  Common reasons it ends up worse: latency, cost, context fragmentation, coordination failures, error propagation.

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Several agents, each with its own tools and instructions, working together on one task.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  A router dispatches; a supervisor orchestrates and aggregates; specialists go deep in a single domain. They can run in parallel or in a hierarchy.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Splitting adds handoff loss and latency. Only split when the tool sets, instructions, or permissions genuinely differ. A single agent with good tools is often more stable.

  ## Interview questions

  1. When should you use multi-agent?
  2. Why is multi-agent sometimes worse?
  3. What's the difference between a supervisor and a router?
  4. How do errors propagate between agents, and how do you stop them?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: Planning
description: 任务分解、plan-and-execute、dynamic planning、replanning、reflection、verification。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  A longer plan isn't a better plan. When execution fails, the agent has to be able to replan.

  ## Must know

  * task decomposition
  * plan-and-execute
  * dynamic planning
  * replanning
  * reflection
  * verification

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Goal → Plan → Execute step
            → Observe
            → Replan / Reflect / Verify
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Breaking a goal into executable steps and revising the plan based on feedback.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Plan-and-execute commits to a plan up front and then runs it. Dynamic planning rethinks at every step. Reflection and verification check whether the result is actually right.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Over-planning burns tokens. A coding agent without verification will confidently ship broken code. This connects to the feedback loop in Agentic Coding.

  ## Interview questions

  1. When do you need an explicit plan, and when is ReAct enough?
  2. What should trigger replanning?
  3. How do you keep reflection from turning into empty self-praise?
  4. Should verification be done by the model, or by tests and rules?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: ReAct
description: Thought → Action → Observation。不要停留在这个名词。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  What the interviewer really wants to know is why you need an agent loop — not whether you can spell out ReAct.

  ## Must know

  Understand the format, and be able to critique it.

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Thought
 ↓
Action
 ↓
Observation
 ↓
Thought
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with actions and uses what it observes to update the next step.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Thought helps break the problem down; Action calls a tool; Observation is feedback from the environment. It's one prompt format for the loop.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Plain ReAct makes step count and cost hard to control. In production you usually see structured tool calling plus an explicit state machine or graph instead of free-text Thoughts.

  ## Interview questions

  1. What problem with single-pass chain-of-thought does ReAct solve?
  2. Why shouldn't you stop at ReAct?
  3. In production, should the Thought text be shown to users?
  4. How does it relate to a LangGraph state machine?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: Agent Reliability
description: max iterations、timeout、retry、circuit breaker、HITL、budget。很大的模块。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Reliability isn't a bonus. Without these, an agent can't go to production.

  ## Must know

  * max iterations
  * timeout
  * retry / exponential backoff
  * circuit breaker
  * tool failure
  * hallucinated tool arguments
  * infinite loops / stuck agents
  * fallback
  * human-in-the-loop
  * budget limits

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
budget / max steps / timeout
        ↓
retry with backoff
        ↓
circuit breaker / fallback model
        ↓
human escalation
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Making sure that when an agent fails, hallucinates, or gets stuck, it can still stop, degrade gracefully, and hand off to a human.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Step counts and budgets are hard limits. Tool-level retries and model-level fallbacks are handled separately. Circuit breakers keep you from hammering downstream services.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  "Your agent loops for 20 steps and costs $0.50": check for a missing stop condition, a tool that keeps failing, a prompt that encourages "try again," and repeated calls with identical arguments.

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you prevent infinite loops?
  2. What if a tool fails?
  3. Should budget limits be measured in tokens, dollars, or steps?
  4. Which failures require a human in the loop, and which can fall back automatically?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

*

title: Agent Security
description: prompt injection、tool injection、exfiltration、excessive agency、sandbox。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Anthropic treats "what can this agent do" and the blast radius when it goes wrong as core engineering questions.

  ## Must know

  * prompt injection / indirect prompt injection
  * tool injection
  * data exfiltration
  * privilege escalation
  * excessive agency
  * sandboxing
  * permission boundaries

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
untrusted content (web, docs, emails)
        ↓
model follows injected instructions?
        ↓
tools / files / network  →  blast radius
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  An agent connects untrusted content to tools that can take real actions, so its attack surface is much larger than a plain chatbot's.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Indirect injection hides inside retrieved documents or web pages. Once the model follows those instructions, it misuses its tools. Containment comes from permissions, sandboxes, and human confirmation.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Least privilege, confirmation for high-risk actions, isolated filesystem and network, and no secrets in the prompt. This connects to [Sandbox](/docs/ai-native/sandbox) and [Context Isolation](/docs/context/isolation).

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you defend against prompt injection?
  2. How does indirect prompt injection differ from direct injection?
  3. How do you limit excessive agency at the product level?
  4. Which tools must require human confirmation?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: Tool Calling
description: function calling、schema、选择、参数校验、执行、retry、timeout、幂等。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  This is the interface that lets an agent actually do things. Tie it to the Tariff / Gemini tools.

  ## Must know

  * function calling
  * tool schema
  * tool selection
  * tool arguments
  * validation
  * execution
  * tool result
  * retry / timeout
  * idempotency

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
LLM → choose tool + args → validate
    → execute → tool result → LLM
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  The model outputs a structured tool name and arguments, the runtime executes the call, and the result gets fed back to the model.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  The schema limits what can be called. Validation blocks hallucinated arguments. Timeouts and retries have to respect idempotency so you don't place an order twice or write the same record twice.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  A tool failure isn't fixed by "just ask the model again." Classify it: bad arguments, downstream 5xx, permissions, timeout. Too many tools lower selection accuracy — that's a Context Construction problem.

  ## Interview questions

  1. How does tool calling work?
  2. How is MCP different from function calling? Details on the MCP page.
  3. How do you prevent hallucinated tool arguments?
  4. Do tools have to be idempotent, and what do you do when they aren't?
  5. What if a tool fails?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: Workflow vs Agent
description: 非常重要的判断题。流程确定就用 workflow。不要为了 Agent 而 Agent。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  A fixed flow is usually cheaper and more predictable. Interview prep material in 2026 stresses this a lot.

  ## Must know

  Draw both control flows, and give an example from your own work where an agent was the wrong call.

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Workflow
A → B → C → D

Agent
A → LLM decides → B
                  ↓
                  C
                  ↓
                  A again
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  A workflow follows a predefined path. An agent lets the model pick the next step at runtime.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Deterministic steps (extract fields → validate → write to the DB) belong in a workflow. You only need an agent when branching depends on an unknown environment and tool results.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  An agent costs you latency, money, and reproducibility. If a workflow solves it, don't wrap it in a layer of "intelligence."

  ## Interview questions

  1. Agent vs workflow?
  2. When should you not use an agent?
  3. How do you mix both in the same product?
  4. Which part of your project is really a workflow?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

*

title: Agent State
description: Conversation ≠ State。长任务 / 后台 / coding agent 尤其重要。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  State can include: task, plan, progress, files, tool results, memory, errors, environment.

  ## Must know

  Only explicit state lets you pause, resume, and run multiple workers.

  ## Mechanism

  ```
  Conversation  =  token history (blows up easily, hard to recover)
  State         =  structured facts about task progress
  ```

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Agent state is serializable work progress — not the chat transcript itself.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Write the plan, the set of files, and failure information to a store or to disk. On resume, rebuild the working set instead of replaying every token.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Background agents must checkpoint. Without state, there's no such thing as long-running reliability.

  ## Interview questions

  1. Why isn't conversation the same as state?
  2. Which fields need to be persisted?
  3. How do you keep the state schema backward-compatible?
  4. How do you make a long-running agent reliable?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

*

title: Agentic Coding
description: Agent 如何知道自己写对了？答案是 feedback loop。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Planning, exploring the repo, editing, running the terminal, testing, debugging, git, verifying, iterating.

  ## Must know

  * planning
  * repository exploration
  * code editing
  * terminal execution
  * testing
  * debugging
  * git
  * verification
  * iteration

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Write
 ↓
Run
 ↓
Test
 ↓
Observe
 ↓
Fix
 ↓
Test
 ↓
Verify
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Treating coding as a loop with feedback from the environment, not a single generation.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Tests, type checks, linters, and repro scripts are all observations. Without them, the model can only "feel" that the code is right.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Evaluation looks at whether the task got done and how many steps it took — not whether the first draft looks nice. Run the tests inside the sandbox.

  ## Interview questions

  1. How does an agent know its code is correct?
  2. How do you verify changes in a repo with no tests?
  3. How do you keep an agent from touching unrelated files?
  4. How do you verify agent-generated code?

title: Claude Code / Codex
description: 理解背后的 architecture，不必成为产品专家。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  At their core, they're agent systems built on LLM + tools + context + state + environment + feedback + safety.

  ## Must know

  Understanding this workflow is enough.

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
User Goal
   ↓
Agent
   ↓
Context
   ↓
Plan
   ↓
Tools
 ├── read file
 ├── edit file
 ├── terminal
 ├── git
 └── tests
   ↓
Observation
   ↓
Agent
   ↓
Verification
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Claude Code and Codex are coding-agent products with repository tools and a verification loop.

description: 接近 context limit 时压缩。真正要答：What information should be preserved?

<Locale lang="en">
  It isn't "summarize the chat so far." Anthropic has written about context resets and the context anxiety models show as they approach the limit.

  ## Must know

  Things that should be preserved, for example:

  * current goal
  * completed tasks
  * important decisions
  * files changed
  * errors
  * unresolved issues
  * tool state
  * user preferences

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Long trajectory
       ↓
Context grows
       ↓
Near context limit
       ↓
Summarize / compact
       ↓
New context
       ↓
Continue
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Proactively compressing context once the trajectory gets long, so the work can continue.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Replace raw observations with a summary plus structured state. When needed, reset the context and inject the key state back in.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Drop the errors and open issues and the agent repeats the same failures. A coding agent has to keep the files it changed and the tests that are still failing.

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you handle context overflow?
  2. What should context compaction preserve?
  3. How do you choose between a context reset and a rolling summary?

title: MCP
description: Host / Client / Server；Tools、Resources、Prompts。JSON-RPC。和 function calling 的区别。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Don't stop at "MCP = Model Context Protocol." The 2026-07-28 spec further standardized primitives, statelessness, authorization, and extensions.

  ## Must know

  * Host / Client / Server
  * Tools / Resources / Prompts
  * JSON-RPC
  * stdio / Streamable HTTP
  * authorization
  * capability negotiation
  * tool discovery
  * security boundary

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Host
 ↓
MCP Client
 ↓
MCP Server
 ├── Tools
 ├── Resources
 └── Prompts
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  MCP is a protocol between models and external capabilities — tools, resources, and prompt templates — rather than one vendor's private function-calling format.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  The host manages sessions and the context boundary. The client connects to servers. Servers expose primitives. Transport is stdio or Streamable HTTP, and messages are JSON-RPC. Both sides negotiate capabilities.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Function calling is the argument shape of a model API; MCP is a protocol for a tool ecosystem and its security boundary. Servers shouldn't see the full conversation by default. Tool discovery lets the harness find capabilities at runtime.

  ## Interview questions

  1. How is MCP different from function calling?
  2. What does each of Tools, Resources, and Prompts solve?
  3. Why must the host be responsible for isolation?
  4. How do you choose between stdio and Streamable HTTP?
  5. What happens when authorization or capability negotiation fails?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

  Running untrusted, model-generated actions inside a restricted environment to limit the blast radius.

title: 数组与哈希
description: 双指针、滑动窗口、前缀和、哈希表。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  ## Patterns

  * Hash maps for **O(1) lookup / counting**
  * Left and right pointers on sorted arrays
  * Sliding window to maintain a range constraint
  * Prefix sums turn a range query into the difference of two prefixes

  ## Skeleton
</Locale>

```ts
function twoSum(nums: number[], target: number) {
  const seen = new Map<number, number>()
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    const need = target - nums[i]
    if (seen.has(need)) return [seen.get(need)!, i]
    seen.set(nums[i], i)
  }
}
```

description: 简单走便宜模型，难的走强模型。fallback、cascade、A/B。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Routing is the lever between cost and quality, and it's also the way into production topics.

  ## Must know

  * routing
  * fallback
  * model cascade
  * A/B testing

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Easy query        → cheap model
Hard query        → strong model
Coding            → specialized model
Summarization     → cheap model
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Sending traffic to different models based on what each request looks like.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Use rules (length, task type), or have a small classifier or small model judge difficulty first. A cascade starts with the cheap model and escalates to the strong one when confidence is low.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Misrouting makes easy questions expensive and breaks hard ones. You need fallbacks and A/B tests. This is different from an agent choosing tools: here you're choosing which brain, not which tool.

  ## Interview questions

  1. What signals do you use to judge how hard a query is?
  2. Compared with always calling the large model, where does a cascade save money and where does it add latency?
  3. What triggers a fallback?
  4. How do you use A/B testing to prove routing didn't hurt quality?

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Forcing the model to produce a structure you can parse and validate, instead of free text.

title: Context Caching
description: Prompt cache ≠ KV cache ≠ semantic cache。非常容易被追问。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  You have to be able to explain the three caches separately.

  ## Must know

  * prompt caching
  * KV cache
  * application-level caching
  * semantic caching

  ## Mechanism

  ```
  Prompt cache     prefix tokens reused across requests on the API / inference side
  KV cache         already-computed K/V reused within a single generation
  Semantic cache   similar questions get a stored answer, possibly skipping the LLM
  ```

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Caches cut repeated computation or repeated billing. Each one sits at a different layer and invalidates under different conditions.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  The KV cache is state inside a single decode. The prompt cache reuses a shared prefix across requests. The semantic cache hits approximately, by embedding similarity.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  If the prefix isn't stable, don't count on prompt caching. User-private data can't go into a shared semantic cache. KV cache blowing up GPU memory is covered on the Inference page.

  ## Interview questions

  1. What's the difference between prompt cache, KV cache, and semantic cache?
  2. What kind of system prompt is a good fit for prompt caching?
  3. How do you prevent false hits in a semantic cache?
  4. Should an application-level cache store answers, retrieval results, or embeddings?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

content:
<Locale lang="en">
  The 2026 MCP architecture is explicit that servers shouldn't see the full conversation by default — the host owns the boundary.

  ## Must know

  With multiple agents or tools, default to the smallest visible set.

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```

  ↓
Tool
  ↓
Agent B
```

<Locale lang="en">

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Every model call and every tool sees only the context needed to finish that step.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  The host enforces isolation; a tool or MCP server gets arguments and authorized resources, not the whole chat transcript.

  Without isolation, prompt injection spreads, data leaks, and permissions get bypassed. This connects to [Agent Security](/docs/agent/security) and [MCP](/docs/ai-native/mcp).

title: Context Window
description: limit、input / output tokens、attention cost、long context degradation、lost-in-the-middle。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Long context isn't free, and quality doesn't keep improving as it gets longer.

  ## Must know

  * context limit
  * input tokens / output tokens
  * attention cost
  * long context degradation
  * lost-in-the-middle

  ## Mechanism

  ```
  input tokens + reserved output ≤ context limit
  attention ~ O(n²)  (sparse variants still get more expensive as n grows)
  ```

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  The maximum number of tokens a model can handle in one call. Input and output usually share that budget or are counted separately.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  As n grows, both attention compute and the KV cache get more expensive. Evidence placed in the middle is more likely to be ignored (lost-in-the-middle).

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Even with a 1M-token window, you shouldn't pour the whole corpus in. Retrieval, compression, and caching are still necessary.

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do input tokens and output tokens affect the window and the bill?
  2. Why does quality degrade with long context?
  3. What does lost-in-the-middle mean for how you order chunks in RAG?
  4. With a huge context window, do you still need RAG?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

title: Agent Evaluation
description: task success、tool 对不对、步数、延迟、成本、trajectory。这是尤其要补的。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  If you only score the final answer, agents that wander all over the place slip through.

  ## Must know

  * Task success
  * Tool selection accuracy
  * Tool argument accuracy
  * Number of steps
  * Latency / Cost
  * Failure rate
  * trajectory evaluation

  ## Mechanism

  ```
  final answer eval     did the task get done?
  trajectory eval       was each tool call / state transition reasonable?
  ```

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Agent evaluation looks at both process and outcome: did it finish the task, did it use the right tools, and how many steps did it take.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  Trajectory eval compares against a gold path or constraints (a tool that must never be called, a verification step that must happen). Succeeding in 20 steps still fails.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Online, monitor success rate, cost, and failure types. Offline, use a fixed task set. Track wrong tool arguments separately from picking the wrong tool.

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you evaluate an agent?
  2. Why do you need trajectory evaluation?
  3. If an agent takes few steps but gets the right answer by luck, is that good?
  4. How do you evaluate coordination quality in a multi-agent system?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

description: golden dataset、benchmark、regression testing、A/B test。

<Locale lang="en">
  Before launch, you must be able to run regressions against a fixed set. A/B tests happen online, but the design starts offline.

  ## Must know

  * golden dataset
  * benchmark
  * regression testing
  * A/B test

  ## Mechanism

  ```
  golden set → run system → scores → pass/fail gate
  online A/B → real users → confirmation takes time
  ```

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Offline: rerun a frozen, labeled set again and again. Online: split traffic and watch real metrics.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  The golden set has to cover failure modes, not just the happy path. Regression tests hook into CI. A/B tests confirm that a change with better offline scores is actually better for users.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  If the set is too small, you end up overfitting to the eval. Production failures need to flow back into the golden set — see Production Eval.

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you build a golden dataset, and who labels it?
  2. How do you combine public benchmarks with a private eval set?
  3. What kinds of changes should block a release?
  4. Offline scores went up but production got worse — what does that tell you?

title: Fine-tuning
description: Full / LoRA / QLoRA / PEFT。高频题：RAG vs Fine-tuning vs Prompt Engineering。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  You need to be able to choose between the three ways of changing model behavior, and tie the choice back to the LLaMA project.

  ## Must know

  * full fine-tuning
  * LoRA
  * QLoRA
  * PEFT
  * adapters

  ## Mechanism

  ```
  Prompt Engineering  →  weights unchanged, change the input
  RAG                 →  weights unchanged, change the context
  Fine-tuning         →  change the weights (or a low-rank adapter)
  ```

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Fine-tuning keeps training on domain data, which changes the model's weights (or an inserted adapter).

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  LoRA freezes the base model and trains small low-rank matrices. QLoRA quantizes the base model first and then applies LoRA, cutting memory further. PEFT is the umbrella term for this family of methods.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Knowledge that changes or needs citations → RAG. Format, tone, or tool-use habits that need to be consistent → small-scale SFT / LoRA. Just phrasing things differently → prompting. They're usually combined; it's not a multiple-choice question.

  ## Interview questions

  1. RAG vs Fine-tuning vs Prompt Engineering?
  2. When do you need full fine-tuning instead of LoRA?
  3. What does QLoRA save, and what does it give up?
  4. How do you avoid catastrophic forgetting?
  5. In your LLaMA-3-8B + QLoRA project, why not just use RAG?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

  Don't start round one with the Transformer paper. Build interview-grade notes in this order: Token → Attention & Transformer → Training → SFT/DPO → Fine-tuning → Inference.

  Every topic has to reach the same bar: **explain it + draw it + answer why + connect it to production**. Don't chase paper count.

  <CardGrid>
    <Card title="Tokenization" description="BPE / WordPiece; how tokens drive context window, latency, and cost." href="/docs/llm/tokenization" />

  </CardGrid>

  ## Plan for this column

  1. Tokenization: why token count matters more than word count; why Chinese and code cost more
  2. Attention & Transformer: go from encoders and decoders to decoder-only, draw a block, explain the KV cache and MHA / MQA / GQA

  4. Fine-tuning anchored on the LLaMA + QLoRA project; answer RAG vs fine-tuning first

</Locale>

title: Inference
description: Prefill / Decode、TTFT / TPOT、KV cache、batching、quantization、speculative decoding。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  In 2026, LLM Engineer interviews use KV cache, quantization, batching, and tokens/sec to tell how deep a candidate really goes.

  ## Must know

  * prefill / decode
  * TTFT / TPOT
  * throughput / latency
  * KV cache
  * batching / continuous batching
  * quantization
  * speculative decoding
  * FlashAttention

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Prefill
Prompt → parallel computation → KV Cache

Decode
Token → KV Cache → Next Token → KV Cache update → Next Token
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Inference has two phases: prefill processes the entire prompt at once, and decode emits tokens one at a time.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  The KV cache avoids recomputing K/V for earlier tokens during decode. Batching packs multiple requests together to raise GPU utilization; continuous batching lets requests join and leave at any step. Quantization lowers numeric precision in exchange for memory and throughput.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  TTFT is mostly about prefill; the typing speed users feel is mostly TPOT. The KV cache grows with batch × layers × sequence length × hidden size, so long sessions run out of GPU memory first. vLLM / PagedAttention fix memory fragmentation. FlashAttention is an IO-aware kernel optimization, not a different model.

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do prefill and decode differ?
  2. What is KV cache? How does it work?
  3. When does KV cache become a bottleneck and how would you solve it?
  4. What drives TTFT, and what drives TPOT?
  5. Why do we need continuous batching?
  6. What are the quality / latency / memory trade-offs of 4-bit quantization?
  7. When does speculative decoding actually help?
  8. Does FlashAttention address compute or memory bandwidth?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

content:
<Locale lang="en">
  This part matters a lot. Be able to draw the whole chain from a pretrained model to one that follows instructions.

  ## Must know

  * SFT
  * RLHF
  * DPO
  * preference data
  * reward model
  * alignment
  * instruction tuning
  * catastrophic forgetting

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Pretraining
     ↓
SFT
     ↓
Preference Optimization
     ↓
RLHF / DPO
     ↓
Instruction Following
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Post-training turns a model that can continue text into one that follows instructions and gives the answers people prefer.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  SFT teaches format and tasks. RLHF uses a reward model plus reinforcement learning; DPO optimizes directly on preference pairs, skipping the explicit reward model and sampling loop.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Data quality and preference coverage decide how the model behaves. Fine-tune too aggressively and you get catastrophic forgetting. In production, most capabilities come from RAG or prompting — not from retraining the base model.

  ## Interview questions

  1. What problem does each of SFT, RLHF, and DPO solve?
  2. Where does preference data come from, and what happens when it's bad?
  3. Why do many teams use DPO instead of full RLHF?
  4. Why can a model lose abilities it had after instruction tuning?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

title: Tokenization
description: BPE / WordPiece / SentencePiece。token 数决定 window、latency、cost。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  A model can't read strings. It only sees a sequence of integers. Tokenization is the step that translates "text a human wrote" into "integers a model can consume."

  It looks like plumbing, but it decides how much context a passage costs, how much a request costs, why Chinese and code behave differently, and why models can't count letters in a word.

  ## Must know

  * how token / vocabulary / token id / embedding relate to each other
  * the trade-offs between word-level, subword-level, and character-level splitting
  * how BPE builds a vocabulary (be able to work it out on a whiteboard)
  * the one formula that separates WordPiece from BPE
  * what SentencePiece solves that the other two can't
  * the vocabulary size trade-off
  * how out-of-vocabulary words are handled, and why byte-level BPE eliminates them
  * the chain from token count to context window, latency, and cost
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Fundamentals

  ### What is tokenization, and why does it matter so much for LLMs?

  Tokenization splits text into smaller units called tokens — **words, subwords, or characters**. Each token is then mapped through a vocabulary to an integer id, and that sequence of integers is what the model actually receives.

  Example:

  ```
  "Hello, world!"
     ↓ split
  ["Hello", ",", " world", "!"]
     ↓ map to ids via the vocabulary
  [9906, 11, 1917, 0]
     ↓ look up the embedding table
  [[0.21, -0.03, ...], [0.08, 0.44, ...], ...]
  ```

  It matters because **every notion of "length" in an LLM is measured in tokens**, not characters:

  * a 128K context window means 128K tokens
  * billing is per token
  * positional encoding indexes token positions
  * KV cache memory grows with token count

  Tokenization is the exchange rate between a piece of text and a dollar amount.

  <MyQuestion q="What exactly are the input and output of tokenization? What are encode and decode, and is tokenization the same as encoding?">
    There are two different input/output pairs here, and they're easy to mix up.

    **Layer 1: tokenization itself** — text in, integers out.

    ```
    Input   raw text                 "Hello, world!"
              ↓ encode (split + vocabulary lookup)
    Output  sequence of token ids    [9906, 11, 1917, 0]
    ```

    **Encode and decode are inverse operations**: encode turns text into ids, decode turns ids back into text. Strictly speaking, tokenization is only the splitting step; a library's `tokenizer.encode()` does split plus vocabulary lookup. So **tokenization is the first step of encoding, not the whole thing** — plenty of sources use the words interchangeably, but separating the two steps makes for a stronger interview answer.

    ```python
    ids = tokenizer.encode("Hello, world!")   # [9906, 11, 1917, 0]
    tokenizer.decode(ids)                     # "Hello, world!"
    ```

    Ideally `decode(encode(text)) == text`, but that isn't automatic. Whether text round-trips exactly depends on whether the tokenizer keeps whitespace information — SentencePiece and byte-level BPE do; classic BPE and WordPiece that pre-split on spaces don't (see Level 2).

    **Layer 2: the input tokens and output tokens of an LLM call** — the two numbers billed separately.

    ```
    everything you send (system prompt, history, tool definitions, retrieved docs, question)
       ↓ tokenizer encode
    input tokens    → read all at once during prefill
       ↓
    output tokens   → token ids the model generates one at a time during decode
       ↓ tokenizer decode (the lookup in reverse: id → string)
    the response text you see
    ```

    So the same tokenizer runs twice: encode on the way in, decode on the way out. Why output tokens come out one at a time, and why they cost more, is covered in Level 3.
  </MyQuestion>

  <Note title="Tokenizer vs. vocabulary">
    The **vocabulary** is a static table mapping every possible token to an id. The **tokenizer** is the tool that does the splitting, and it ships with the vocabulary inside. The vocabulary is the dictionary; the tokenizer is the person working with that dictionary in hand.
  </Note>

  <MyQuestion q="How do tokenization and the tokenizer relate? Does the tokenizer contain the vocabulary, and where do the splitting rules come from?">
    **A process and its tool.** Tokenization is the process of splitting and numbering; the tokenizer is the tool that carries it out — the way chopping relates to the knife.

    **The tokenizer does contain the vocabulary**, and it's a core part, not an add-on. A complete tokenizer bundles two things:

    ```
    Tokenizer = ① splitting rules (how to cut text into token strings)
              + ② vocabulary (token string ↔ integer id)
    ```

    For BPE, training produces exactly two files: `merges.txt` (the merge order) and `vocab.json` (e.g. `{"low": 1024, "est</w>": 1025}`, ids for illustration only). At inference the order is fixed:

    1. Apply the merge rules to cut the text into token strings: `"lowest"` → `["low", "est</w>"]`
    2. Look those strings up in the vocabulary to get ids: → `[1024, 1025]`

    The order in which step 1 applies the merge rules (it isn't left to right) is covered in Level 2.

    **The algorithm learns the rules — not the other way around.** The layers are easy to flip, so keep them straight:

    ```
    Layer 1  method / algorithm   BPE, WordPiece, Unigram — how the rules get learned
    Layer 2  training artifacts   merges.txt + vocab.json — what was learned on a given corpus
    Layer 3  inference            apply the Layer 2 rules to new text
    ```

    It isn't "the splitting rules define BPE"; it's "BPE, run on a corpus, produces the splitting rules." For how that learning works, see the BPE walkthrough in Level 2.

    What gets stored varies by algorithm: BPE keeps a merge table plus the vocabulary; WordPiece keeps only the vocabulary and splits by greedy longest match at inference; Unigram keeps a vocabulary with a probability score per token and picks the most likely segmentation. The rules-plus-vocabulary structure is the same.
  </MyQuestion>

  ### How do token, token id, and embedding relate?

  These get conflated constantly, but they're three distinct stages of a pipeline:

  | Stage | Output | Carries meaning? |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Tokenization | a **string fragment** like `" world"` | no |
  | Vocabulary lookup | an **integer id** like `1917` | no — it's just a row number |
  | Embedding | a **vector** like `[0.21, -0.03, ...]` | yes — meaning starts here |

  The key point: **token ids carry no semantics**. Ids 1917 and 1918 are numerically adjacent but may represent totally unrelated words. Meaning is learned entirely by the embedding layer — a `[vocab_size, hidden_dim]` matrix that the token id indexes into.

  <Note title="Why this distinction matters in interviews" type="tip">
    If you're asked "how does tokenization capture meaning," the correct answer is that it doesn't. Tokenization only splits and numbers; meaning is the job of embedding plus attention downstream. Getting this wrong signals shaky fundamentals.
  </Note>

  ### Why bill per token instead of per word or per character?

  Because the token is the model's real unit of compute. Each forward pass costs in proportion to the number of tokens in the sequence — regardless of whether a token is a five-letter English word or a single Chinese character.

  An intuition (measured with cl100k):

  ```
  "the"          3 chars    1 word   1 token
  "strawberry"   10 chars   1 word   3 tokens   ["str", "aw", "berry"]
  "中国"          2 chars    1 word   1 token
  ```

  Counting characters, the cost ratio would be 3 : 10 : 2; counting words, 1 : 1 : 1. The model's actual compute is 1 : 3 : 1. Neither lines up — only tokens do.

  <Note title="This also explains a classic failure" type="tip">
    "Why can't an LLM count the r's in strawberry?" Because the model never saw the ten characters `s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y`. It saw three integers standing for `["str", "aw", "berry"]`. Letter-level information was destroyed at the tokenization step.
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Tokenization methods

  ### What are the main approaches, and what do they trade off?

  Three families, all trading **vocabulary size** against **sequence length**:

  | Method | Example | Vocab size | Sequence length | Main problem |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Word-level | `"natural language processing"` → `["natural", "language", "processing"]` | huge (100k+) | short | severe OOV: unseen words become `[UNK]` and lose all information |
  | **Subword-level** | `"tokenization"` → `["token", "ization"]` | moderate (30k–200k) | moderate | the standard choice, no fatal flaw |
  | Character-level | `"cat"` → `["c", "a", "t"]` | tiny (hundreds) | very long | sequences blow up attention's O(n²) cost |

  Subword won because it takes the good half of both: **frequent words stay whole (`"the"` is one token) while rare words break into meaningful pieces (`"unhappiness"` → `["un", "happiness"]`)**. No OOV, no sequence explosion.

  ### How does BPE work? Work it out by hand

  The whole idea in one sentence: **repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, until the vocabulary reaches its target size.**

  Say the training corpus contains only four words, with these counts:

  ```
  low     × 5
  lower   × 2
  newest  × 6
  widest  × 3
  ```

  **Step 0: split everything into characters** (`</w>` marks end of word)

  ```
  l o w </w>          × 5
  l o w e r </w>      × 2
  n e w e s t </w>    × 6
  w i d e s t </w>    × 3
  ```

  **Step 1: count every adjacent pair**

  ```
  (e, s) = 6 + 3 = 9   ← highest
  (s, t) = 6 + 3 = 9
  (t, </w>) = 6 + 3 = 9
  (w, e) = 2 + 6 = 8
  (l, o) = 5 + 2 = 7
  (o, w) = 5 + 2 = 7
  ...
  ```

  **Step 2: merge the most frequent pair**, `(e, s)` → `es`

  ```
  n e w es t </w>     × 6
  w i d es t </w>     × 3
  ```

  **Step 3: repeat.** Now `(es, t) = 9` is highest, so merge it into `est`:

  ```
  n e w est </w>      × 6
  w i d est </w>      × 3
  ```

  Continuing:

  | Round | Merged pair | New token | Corpus becomes |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 1 | (e, s) | `es` | `n e w es t` / `w i d es t` |
  | 2 | (es, t) | `est` | `n e w est` / `w i d est` |
  | 3 | (est, `</w>`) | `est</w>` | `n e w est</w>` / `w i d est</w>` |
  | 4 | (l, o) | `lo` | `lo w` / `lo w e r` |
  | 5 | (lo, w) | `low` | `low` / `low e r` |

  Stop when the vocabulary hits its target size. The final vocabulary contains **learned** subword units like `low`, `est</w>`, and `er</w>`.

  **At inference time nothing is counted.** The merge rules learned during training are simply replayed in the same order. So a tokenizer is fully deterministic: same text, same tokenizer, always the same split.

  <Note title="Why BPE handles unseen words">
    Given `"lowest"`, which never appeared in training, BPE doesn't emit `[UNK]` — it assembles `["low", "est</w>"]` from existing merge rules. Almost no information is lost. That's the core advantage of subword over word-level.
  </Note>

  <MyQuestion q="How does the vocabulary relate to an algorithm like BPE, and what decides the vocabulary size?">
    **The vocabulary grows out of training step by step; it isn't designed first and then handed to the algorithm.** Look back at the walkthrough above:

    ```
    Step 0    vocab = every single character   {l, o, w, e, r, n, s, t, i, d, </w>}
    Round 1   merge (e, s) → es                vocab + es
    Round 2   merge (es, t) → est              vocab + est
    Round 3   merge (est, </w>) → est</w>      vocab + est</w>
    ```

    Every merge adds exactly one entry. So `merges.txt` and `vocab.json` aren't two independently designed pieces — they're two records of the same training run: one logs the merge order, the other lists every token that exists at the end, with its id.

    **Vocabulary size is a hyperparameter set before training** (the main one; pre-tokenization rules and special tokens are others). The algorithm keeps merging until it hits that number:

    ```
    target vocabulary size (you choose it)
       ↓ determines
    how many merge rounds run
       ↓ determines
    which tokens exist, and how coarse or fine the splits are
    ```

    A real example that adds up: GPT-2's vocabulary is 50,257 = 256 base bytes + 50,000 merges + 1 special token (`<|endoftext|>`).

    In one line: **the algorithm is how to learn, the vocabulary size is the parameter you give it, and the vocabulary is what comes out** — method → parameter → output. That's one reason GPT-2 (50k) and LLaMA 3 (128k), both BPE-family tokenizers, split the same sentence into different numbers of tokens; their training corpora and pre-tokenization rules differ too (see Level 3). For how to pick the size, see "How do you choose a vocabulary size?" below.
  </MyQuestion>

  <MyQuestion q="How are merge rules actually used at inference? Once training produces a vocabulary, why not just split using the vocabulary?">
    **Because the vocabulary alone isn't enough — you also need the merge order.** The vocabulary only answers "which tokens are valid." A word often has several splits that are all valid, and an unordered set can't tell you which to pick. The **order (rank)** of the merge rules can.

    Here's how BPE applies the rules at inference:

    1. Break the word into base units (characters or bytes)
    2. Among all current adjacent pairs, find the one whose rule was **learned earliest** (lowest rank) — wherever it sits, not just the leftmost
    3. Merge it and go back to step 2, until no pair matches any rule

    A counterexample shows why the order is required. Say the rules, in learned order, are:

    ```
    rule 1 (learned first): (b, c) → bc
    rule 2                : (a, b) → ab
    ```

    A new word splits into `a b c a`:

    ```
    merge by rank (correct)          merge the first match left to right (wrong)
    a b c a                          a b c a
    (a,b)=rule 2, (b,c)=rule 1       hits (a,b) first and merges it
    → merge (b,c) first              → ab c a
    a bc a, no rule applies, stop    no rule applies, stop
    ["a", "bc", "a"]                 ["ab", "c", "a"]
    ```

    Every token in both results is in the vocabulary, yet the splits differ. Inference has to reproduce the split used in training; otherwise the model gets a token sequence it has barely seen, and quality drops. That rank order is what "replayed in the same order" above refers to.

    In one line: **the vocabulary answers "what counts as a valid token"; the merge order answers "when several merges are valid, which goes first."**
  </MyQuestion>

  ### How does WordPiece differ from BPE?

  The procedure is nearly identical. **Only the criterion for choosing which pair to merge differs:**

  ```
  BPE:        pick the pair with the highest freq(u, v)
  WordPiece:  pick the pair with the highest freq(u, v) / (freq(u) × freq(v))
  ```

  The denominator **penalizes combinations whose parts are already common on their own**.

  Concretely: suppose `e` and `s` are each extremely frequent (10,000 occurrences apiece) and appear adjacently 9 times. BPE sees 9 and considers it decent. WordPiece computes `9 / (10000 × 10000)` — a tiny score — and concludes they merely happen to sit next to each other rather than forming a meaningful unit.

  Conversely, if `happi` and `ness` each occur only 10 times but 9 of those are together, WordPiece scores that very highly, because the parts are **strongly bound** and merging them into `happiness` is semantically justified.

  In one line: **BPE looks at raw frequency, WordPiece looks at correlation.**

  <Note title="WordPiece's ## prefix">
    BERT-family tokenizers produce tokens like `##er` and `##ing`. The `##` means "this token can only appear as a suffix, never standalone." For example `"playing"` → `["play", "##ing"]`.
  </Note>

  <MyQuestion q="How does WordPiece actually run? Can you work it through with numbers?">
    **Training: the same loop as BPE, with a different score for picking the pair.**

    ```
    ① count every adjacent pair
    ② pick the highest-scoring pair        ← the only step that differs
    ③ merge it and add it to the vocabulary
    ④ repeat until the vocabulary hits its target size
    ```

    Here's the example above with numbers that actually separate the two (simplified for hand calculation):

    | Pair | Individual counts | Adjacent count | What BPE scores | WordPiece score |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | (e, s) | 10000 / 10000 | 900 | **900** | 900 / (10000 × 10000) = 0.000009 |
    | (happi, ness) | 10 / 10 | 9 | 9 | 9 / (10 × 10) = **0.09** |

    BPE picks `(e, s)` because 900 is the largest count. WordPiece picks `(happi, ness)` because its score is 10,000x higher. The formula asks: "relative to how often each piece appears on its own, do these two appear together a lot?" `e` and `s` are everywhere, so 900 co-occurrences mean little; `happi` appears 10 times and is followed by `ness` in 9 of them, so they really are one unit.

    **Inference: no merge rules — greedy longest match against the vocabulary.** WordPiece stores only the vocabulary (word-internal pieces carry a `##` prefix). It scans each word left to right and takes the **longest** piece the vocabulary contains:

    ```
    vocabulary (excerpt): un, ##happi, ##ness, ##h, ##a, ...
    "unhappiness"
      longest match from the start             → "un"
      remaining "happiness", longest ## piece  → "##happi"
      remaining "ness"                         → "##ness"
    result: ["un", "##happi", "##ness"]
    ```

    If nothing matches at some step, the whole word becomes `[UNK]` — which is why BERT-style tokenizers can still emit `[UNK]` while byte-level BPE can't (see OOV below).
  </MyQuestion>

  ### What problem does SentencePiece solve?

  Both methods above assume something: **first split the sentence into words by whitespace, then split subwords inside each word.** That assumption holds for English and fails completely for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, which have no spaces at all.

  SentencePiece's answer: **train directly on raw text and treat the space as just another character** (written `▁`, U+2581).

  Example:

  ```
  "Hello世界"  →  ["▁He", "llo", "▁世", "界"]
  ```

  The `▁` in `▁He` is that space. Two benefits follow:

  1. **No pre-tokenization needed** — mixed Chinese/English, Japanese, code, and messy social-media text all go through the same path
  2. **Fully reversible** — concatenate the tokens, swap `▁` back to a space, and you recover the original text exactly. Classic BPE and WordPiece discard whitespace information (they pre-split on spaces) and need extra rules to detokenize

  Underneath, SentencePiece can run either BPE or a Unigram language model. T5 and LLaMA 1 / 2 both use it.

  <MyQuestion q="Is one of these methods better than the others? Which one do current LLMs use?">
    **It isn't a ranking — each one fixes a weakness of the one before**, and the right choice depends on the use case. First, untangle three dimensions that often get lumped together:

    ```
    algorithm (how the vocabulary is learned)   BPE, WordPiece, Unigram LM
    base unit                                   characters / bytes (byte-level)
    tool / implementation                       SentencePiece, tiktoken, Hugging Face tokenizers
    ```

    SentencePiece isn't a third algorithm; it's a training framework that needs no pre-tokenization and runs BPE or Unigram inside. Unigram works in the opposite direction from BPE: start from a large candidate vocabulary and, each round, drop the tokens whose removal hurts corpus likelihood the least, until the target size is reached.

    | Method | Weakness it fixes | Limitation |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | BPE | Statistical merging solves OOV and vocabulary blow-up | Merges by raw frequency, so very common pieces can mislead it |
    | WordPiece | A correlation score merges more meaningful pieces | Still needs pre-tokenization; longest match can fall back to `[UNK]` |
    | SentencePiece (BPE / Unigram) | No reliance on spaces; handles CJK and mixed text uniformly; reversible | Doesn't define the merge criterion itself — results depend on the algorithm and corpus inside |

    **What major models use** (per public information):

    ```
    GPT-4 / GPT-4o     byte-level BPE (tiktoken: cl100k_base / o200k_base)
    LLaMA 1 / 2        SentencePiece + BPE (32k, character-level + byte fallback)
    LLaMA 3            byte-level BPE (tiktoken-based, 128k)
    Gemma / Gemini     SentencePiece
    BERT               WordPiece
    T5                 SentencePiece + Unigram
    Claude             proprietary, unpublished; count tokens with the official token-counting API
    ```

    The trend is clear: **recent LLMs have largely converged on byte-level BPE with large vocabularies.** Byte-level guarantees any text can be encoded (see the byte-level BPE Q\&A under OOV below), and a large vocabulary fits the same text into fewer tokens.
  </MyQuestion>

  ### How do you choose a vocabulary size?

  A direct trade-off with no universal answer:

  | | Small vocab (e.g. 32k) | Large vocab (e.g. 200k) |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Embedding parameters | fewer, saves memory | many (`vocab_size × hidden_dim`, potentially hundreds of millions) |
  | Output softmax | fast | slow — probabilities over the whole vocabulary |
  | Tokens per passage | more, eats context | fewer, fits more into context |
  | Rare words / multilingual | shredded into pieces | well covered |

  Some real numbers for calibration:

  ```
  BERT-base      30,522
  LLaMA 1 / 2    32,000
  GPT-2          50,257
  cl100k_base    100,277   (GPT-4 / GPT-3.5-turbo)
  LLaMA 3        128,256
  o200k_base     200,019   (GPT-4o)
  ```

  The trend is clear: **vocabularies are growing.** A larger vocabulary compresses the same text into fewer tokens, which pays off more and more in the long-context era, while the extra embedding parameters are now negligible next to total model size.

  ### How are out-of-vocabulary words handled?

  With subword tokenization, OOV is largely a solved problem, but the full answer has three layers:

  1. **Subword splitting** (the standard): unseen words decompose into known subwords, e.g. `"tokenization"` → `["token", "ization"]`, preserving most information
  2. **Byte-level fallback**: GPT-family models use byte-level BPE, where the smallest unit is a **byte**, not a character. Since any text can be represented as bytes, **OOV is impossible in principle** — emoji, mojibake, and binary strings all encode
  3. **An `[UNK]` token** (legacy): drop it entirely and lose the information. Modern tokenizers rarely need this

  <MyQuestion q="How does byte-level BPE differ from regular BPE? How does it handle Chinese, and how do today's large vocabularies make Chinese cheaper?">
    **Only one thing differs: the unit merging starts from.** The merge algorithm is exactly the walkthrough above; what changes is what step 0 splits text into:

    | | Character-level BPE (regular) | Byte-level BPE |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Step 0 splits into | Unicode characters | UTF-8 bytes |
    | Starting set | whatever characters the corpus contains — thousands to tens of thousands, **open-ended** | always 256, **closed** |
    | An unseen character | OOV, becomes `[UNK]` | can't happen |
    | Cost | large starting set, still hits OOV | languages rare in the corpus get split into byte fragments |
    | Used by | early machine-translation BPE; LLaMA 1 / 2 (with byte fallback) | GPT models from GPT-2 on (tiktoken), LLaMA 3 |

    **Why does character-level still hit OOV?** The walkthrough used English, so step 0 had a dozen letters and the problem stayed hidden. But Unicode has about 150,000 characters and adds emoji every year, so no corpus covers them all. A rare character or a brand-new emoji has no slot even at step 0, so it becomes `[UNK]`. It's the word-level OOV problem again, one level down: smaller, not gone.

    **Why do bytes fix it?** All text is stored as UTF-8 bytes, and a byte has only 256 possible values. Whatever new character shows up is still some combination of those 256, so "a base unit we've never seen" can't happen.

    Take `中` as an example:

    ```
    "A"   → 1 byte in UTF-8    0x41
    "中"  → 3 bytes in UTF-8   0xE4 0xB8 0xAD

    character-level:  中 is one unit at step 0
                      Chinese in the corpus → can keep merging with other characters
                      no Chinese at all     → 中 isn't in the vocabulary → [UNK]

    byte-level:       中 is three units at step 0: E4 / B8 / AD
                      Chinese in the corpus → the 3 bytes merge into 1 token
                      no Chinese at all     → stays as 3 byte fragments, but still encodes
    ```

    **The middle ground, byte fallback**: LLaMA 1 / 2 use character-level SentencePiece BPE, but the vocabulary also carries 256 byte tokens (`<0x00>` … `<0xFF>`). Known characters split as characters; only unknown ones fall back to bytes. So it never hits OOV either.

    **Byte-level guarantees text can be encoded, not that it's encoded efficiently.** Efficiency comes down to two things, and that's exactly why large vocabularies help Chinese so much:

    1. **A bigger vocabulary means more merge rounds.** GPT-2 is 256 bytes + 50,000 merges. Merges go to the most frequent pairs; GPT-2's corpus was mostly English, so English pieces took most of the budget and plenty of Chinese characters ran out before their 3 bytes were merged. At 100k or 200k entries, the extra merges finally reach whole Chinese characters, even common words
    2. **More Chinese in the tokenizer's training corpus.** The team chooses that corpus, and multilingual tokenizers usually raise the share of Chinese, Japanese, and so on on purpose. Frequent pieces get merged earlier. A bigger vocabulary trained on almost-all-English text would help Chinese much less

    Both effects together, measured with tiktoken:

    ```
                      "中国"                         a 70-character Chinese passage
    GPT-2   (50k)     3 tokens: 中 / E5 9B / BD      143 tokens (~2 per character)
    cl100k  (100k)    1 token                        82 tokens (~1.2 per character)
    o200k   (200k)    1 token                        50 tokens (~0.7 per character)
    ```

    In GPT-2, `中` already merged into a whole character while `国` stayed as two byte fragments: the more common a character, the earlier it gets a merge.

    A side effect you can actually see: when streaming, if a character is split across two tokens and the client doesn't buffer bytes, the first half can't be decoded yet and briefly shows up as `�`.

    For estimating Chinese token counts, and why "Chinese is always more expensive" is wrong, see Level 3 and Traps.
  </MyQuestion>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Engineering impact

  ### How does token count propagate into latency and cost?

  This chain is the single most important thing on this page:
</Locale>

<Locale lang="zh">
  拆开说：

  * **Prefill 阶段**：模型要一次性处理完整个 prompt。这部分可以并行，但 attention 里的 `Q·Kᵀ` 是 n×n 的矩阵，所以计算量随 n 平方增长。prompt 越长，首 token 出来得越慢（TTFT 越高）
  * **KV Cache**：每个 token 都要缓存它的 K 和 V 向量，显存占用随 n **线性**增长。显存被吃满，单卡能同时跑的请求数就下降，摊到每个请求的成本就上升
  * **Context Window**：装不下就必须截断或压缩，这时候才需要 [Context Engineering](/docs/context) 那一整套东西

  ### 为什么 output token 比 input token 贵好几倍？

  因为两者的计算方式根本不同：

  ```
  Input token  → Prefill  → 一次性并行处理完 → 单位成本低
  Output token → Decode   → 一次只能生成 1 个 → 无法并行 → 单位成本高
  ```

  生成 100 个 output token，意味着要跑 100 次前向传播，每次都要重新读一遍全部模型权重。而 100 个 input token 只需要 1 次前向传播就全处理完了。

  **工程结论：想省钱和降延迟，先砍 output 长度，再砍 input 长度。** 一个「请简短回答」的指令，省下来的钱通常比压缩 prompt 更多。

  <Note title="这也解释了 prompt caching 为什么有用" type="tip">
    既然 prefill 的成本来自「重新处理一遍 prompt」，那把不变的前缀（system prompt、few-shot 例子）缓存下来，就能直接跳过这部分计算。这就是 [Caching](/docs/context/caching) 的原理。
  </Note>

  <MyQuestion q="为什么 output token 只能一个一个生成？不能像 input 那样并行，或者一次生成好几个吗？">
    **关键区别：input 是已经存在的，output 是还不存在的。**

    * **Prefill**：你发出请求时，prompt 里每个 token 都已经确定。模型可以把它们放进一次前向计算，所有位置并行算完（causal mask 保证每个位置只看它前面的 token）
    * **Decode**：LLM 是自回归模型，生成第 k 个 token 时，输入必须包含第 1 … k−1 个 token 的**真实结果**：

    ```
    生成第 1 个：看 [prompt]
    生成第 2 个：看 [prompt] + 第 1 个     ← 第 1 个要先算完、采样出来才存在
    生成第 3 个：看 [prompt] + 第 1、2 个
    ```

    这是严格的先后依赖：不是「数据都在、只是还没算」，而是下一步的输入要等上一步采样完才出现。

    **为什么不能一次猜好几个？** 可以猜，但第 5 个 token 就得建立在「假设的」第 2–4 个上。如果第 3 个实际采样出 "dog"，而你假设的是 "cat"，第 5 个就接不上了。所以标准 decode 必须串行。

    工程上有两种「绕开」的办法，都不违反这个依赖：

    * **跨请求并行**：同一时刻把很多用户的 decode 拼进一个 batch（continuous batching），但每条序列仍然一步只前进一个 token
    * **Speculative decoding**：让一个小模型先草拟几个 token，大模型用**一次**前向计算并行验证，从第一个不对的位置丢弃重来。猜中得越多越省时间，而且输出分布和逐个生成完全一样

    细节见 [Inference](/docs/llm/inference)。
  </MyQuestion>

  ### 为什么同一段文本在不同模型上 token 数不同？

  因为**每个模型有自己的 tokenizer 和词表**，而且 tokenizer 是和模型权重一起训练 / 发布的，不能混用。

  这意味着一个很实际的工程陷阱：

  > 你在 GPT-4 上测出某个 prompt 是 1200 token，换到另一个模型上，它可能是 950 或 1400 token。**拿旧的 token 数 × 新的单价，算出来的成本是错的。**

  做跨模型成本对比时，必须用**各自的 tokenizer 重新数一遍**。

  ### 中文 / 代码场景怎么估算 token？

  不要背固定比例，**要实测**：同一段中文换个 tokenizer，token 数能差将近 3 倍（实测见 Level 2 byte-level BPE 那条问答）。粗略的量感：

  ```
  英文     ≈ 1 token / 0.75 词    （约 4 个字符 1 个 token）
  中文     cl100k 每字约 1.2 个 token，o200k 每字约 0.7 个
  代码     缩进、符号很吃 token，通常比同长度英文散文贵
  ```

  实测方法：
</Locale>

```python
# OpenAI
import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4o")
print(len(enc.encode("your text")))

# open models on HuggingFace
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-3-8B")
print(len(tok.encode("your text")))
```

<Locale lang="en">
  <Note title="Direct consequence for RAG" type="tip">
    Chunk size must be defined in **tokens**, not characters. The same "500" applied to Chinese versus English can differ by 2x in actual tokens, throwing off your context budget. See [Chunking](/docs/rag/chunking).
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note title="A token is not a word, and not a character either" type="warning">
    A token can be a whole word, a subword, a single character, punctuation, or even a **leading space** — `" the"` and `"the"` are two different tokens in most tokenizers. Saying "one Chinese character equals one token" invites an immediate follow-up.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Don't claim Chinese is always more expensive" type="danger">
    That's an outdated conclusion. The small vocabularies of the GPT-2 / GPT-3 era handled Chinese badly, about 2 tokens per character on average; with o200k the same passage takes about 0.7. The accurate framing: **token efficiency depends on vocabulary size and on how well that language is represented in the tokenizer's training corpus.** Measure, don't recite.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Latency doesn't scale linearly with total tokens" type="warning">
    Input goes through prefill and parallelizes; output goes through decode and doesn't. Latency is driven mainly by **output length**, not total token count. "Longer prompts are slower" is only half true.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Tokenization produces no semantics" type="warning">
    Its output is an **integer id** — purely a lookup row number. Meaning appears at the embedding layer. Asked "how does tokenization understand meaning," the right answer is that it doesn't.
  </Note>

  ## Level 1 · Fundamentals

  ### What is tokenization, and why does it matter so much for LLMs?

  Tokenization splits text into smaller units called tokens —

. Each token is then mapped through a vocabulary to an integer id, and that sequence of integers is what the model actually receives.

  Example:

  ```
  "Hello, world!"
     ↓ split
  ["Hello", ",", " world", "!"]
     ↓ map to ids via the vocabulary
  [9906, 11, 1917, 0]
     ↓ look up the embedding table
  [[0.21, -0.03, ...], [0.08, 0.44, ...], ...]
  ```

  It matters because
Encode and decode are inverse operations
tokenization is the first step of encoding, not the whole thing
Layer 2: the input tokens and output tokens of an LLM call
The tokenizer does contain the vocabulary
The algorithm learns the rules — not the other way around.

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Tokenization methods

  ### What are the main approaches, and what do they trade off?

  Three families, all trading

:

  | Method | Example | Vocab size | Sequence length | Main problem |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Word-level | `"natural language processing"` → `["natural", "language", "processing"]` | huge (100k+) | short | severe OOV: unseen words become `[UNK]` and lose all information |
  |

| `"tokenization"` → `["token", "ization"]` | moderate (30k–200k) | moderate | the standard choice, no fatal flaw |
  | Character-level | `"cat"` → `["c", "a", "t"]` | tiny (hundreds) | very long | sequences blow up attention's O(n²) cost |

  Subword won because it takes the good half of both:

. No OOV, no sequence explosion.

  ### How does BPE work? Work it out by hand

  The whole idea in one sentence:

Say the training corpus contains only four words, with these counts:

  ```
  low     × 5
  lower   × 2
  newest  × 6
  widest  × 3
  ```

(`</w>` marks end of word)

  ```
  l o w </w>          × 5
  l o w e r </w>      × 2
  n e w e s t </w>    × 6
  w i d e s t </w>    × 3
  ```

, `(e, s)` → `es`

  ```
  n e w es t </w>     × 6
  w i d es t </w>     × 3
  ```

Now `(es, t) = 9` is highest, so merge it into `est`:

  ```
  n e w est </w>      × 6
  w i d est </w>      × 3
  ```

  Continuing:

  | Round | Merged pair | New token | Corpus becomes |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 1 | (e, s) | `es` | `n e w es t` / `w i d es t` |
  | 2 | (es, t) | `est` | `n e w est` / `w i d est` |
  | 3 | (est, `</w>`) | `est</w>` | `n e w est</w>` / `w i d est</w>` |
  | 4 | (l, o) | `lo` | `lo w` / `lo w e r` |
  | 5 | (lo, w) | `low` | `low` / `low e r` |

  Stop when the vocabulary hits its target size. The final vocabulary contains

The merge rules learned during training are simply replayed in the same order. So a tokenizer is fully deterministic: same text, same tokenizer, always the same split.

  <Note title="Why BPE handles unseen words">
    Given `"lowest"`, which never appeared in training, BPE doesn't emit `[UNK]` — it assembles `["low", "est</w>"]` from existing merge rules. Almost no information is lost. That's the core advantage of subword over word-level.
  </Note>

  <MyQuestion q="How does the vocabulary relate to an algorithm like BPE, and what decides the vocabulary size?">

Look back at the walkthrough above:

    ```
    Step 0    vocab = every single character   {l, o, w, e, r, n, s, t, i, d, </w>}
    Round 1   merge (e, s) → es                vocab + es
    Round 2   merge (es, t) → est              vocab + est
    Round 3   merge (est, </w>) → est</w>      vocab + est</w>
    ```

    Every merge adds exactly one entry. So `merges.txt` and `vocab.json` aren't two independently designed pieces — they're two records of the same training run: one logs the merge order, the other lists every token that exists at the end, with its id.

(the main one; pre-tokenization rules and special tokens are others). The algorithm keeps merging until it hits that number:

    ```
    target vocabulary size (you choose it)
       ↓ determines
    how many merge rounds run
       ↓ determines
    which tokens exist, and how coarse or fine the splits are
    ```

    A real example that adds up: GPT-2's vocabulary is 50,257 = 256 base bytes + 50,000 merges + 1 special token (`<|endoftext|>`).

    In one line:

— method → parameter → output. That's one reason GPT-2 (50k) and LLaMA 3 (128k), both BPE-family tokenizers, split the same sentence into different numbers of tokens; their training corpora and pre-tokenization rules differ too (see Level 3). For how to pick the size, see "How do you choose a vocabulary size?" below.
  </MyQuestion>

  <MyQuestion q="How are merge rules actually used at inference? Once training produces a vocabulary, why not just split using the vocabulary?">
The vocabulary only answers "which tokens are valid." A word often has several splits that are all valid, and an unordered set can't tell you which to pick. The

of the merge rules can.

    Here's how BPE applies the rules at inference:

    1. Break the word into base units (characters or bytes)
    2. Among all current adjacent pairs, find the one whose rule was

(lowest rank) — wherever it sits, not just the leftmost
    3. Merge it and go back to step 2, until no pair matches any rule

    A counterexample shows why the order is required. Say the rules, in learned order, are:

    ```
    rule 1 (learned first): (b, c) → bc
    rule 2                : (a, b) → ab
    ```

    A new word splits into `a b c a`:

    ```
    merge by rank (correct)          merge the first match left to right (wrong)
    a b c a                          a b c a
    (a,b)=rule 2, (b,c)=rule 1       hits (a,b) first and merges it
    → merge (b,c) first              → ab c a
    a bc a, no rule applies, stop    no rule applies, stop
    ["a", "bc", "a"]                 ["ab", "c", "a"]
    ```

    Every token in both results is in the vocabulary, yet the splits differ. Inference has to reproduce the split used in training; otherwise the model gets a token sequence it has barely seen, and quality drops. That rank order is what "replayed in the same order" above refers to.
