  ### How does WordPiece differ from BPE?

  The procedure is nearly identical.

```
  BPE:        pick the pair with the highest freq(u, v)
  WordPiece:  pick the pair with the highest freq(u, v) / (freq(u) × freq(v))
  ```

  The denominator

.

  Concretely: suppose `e` and `s` are each extremely frequent (10,000 occurrences apiece) and appear adjacently 9 times. BPE sees 9 and considers it decent. WordPiece computes `9 / (10000 × 10000)` — a tiny score — and concludes they merely happen to sit next to each other rather than forming a meaningful unit.

  Conversely, if `happi` and `ness` each occur only 10 times but 9 of those are together, WordPiece scores that very highly, because the parts are

and merging them into `happiness` is semantically justified.

  In one line:

<Note title="WordPiece's ## prefix">
    BERT-family tokenizers produce tokens like `##er` and `##ing`. The `##` means "this token can only appear as a suffix, never standalone." For example `"playing"` → `["play", "##ing"]`.
  </Note>

  <MyQuestion q="How does WordPiece actually run? Can you work it through with numbers?">

```
    ① count every adjacent pair
    ② pick the highest-scoring pair        ← the only step that differs
    ③ merge it and add it to the vocabulary
    ④ repeat until the vocabulary hits its target size
    ```

    Here's the example above with numbers that actually separate the two (simplified for hand calculation):

    | Pair | Individual counts | Adjacent count | What BPE scores | WordPiece score |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | (e, s) | 10000 / 10000 | 900 |

|

    BPE picks `(e, s)` because 900 is the largest count. WordPiece picks `(happi, ness)` because its score is 10,000x higher. The formula asks: "relative to how often each piece appears on its own, do these two appear together a lot?" `e` and `s` are everywhere, so 900 co-occurrences mean little; `happi` appears 10 times and is followed by `ness` in 9 of them, so they really are one unit.
WordPiece stores only the vocabulary (word-internal pieces carry a `##` prefix). It scans each word left to right and takes the

piece the vocabulary contains:

    ```
    vocabulary (excerpt): un, ##happi, ##ness, ##h, ##a, ...
    "unhappiness"
      longest match from the start             → "un"
      remaining "happiness", longest ## piece  → "##happi"
      remaining "ness"                         → "##ness"
    result: ["un", "##happi", "##ness"]
    ```

    If nothing matches at some step, the whole word becomes `[UNK]` — which is why BERT-style tokenizers can still emit `[UNK]` while byte-level BPE can't (see OOV below).
  </MyQuestion>

  ### What problem does SentencePiece solve?

  Both methods above assume something:

That assumption holds for English and fails completely for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, which have no spaces at all.

  SentencePiece's answer:

(written `▁`, U+2581).

  Example:

  ```
  "Hello世界"  →  ["▁He", "llo", "▁世", "界"]
  ```

  The `▁` in `▁He` is that space. Two benefits follow:

  1.

— mixed Chinese/English, Japanese, code, and messy social-media text all go through the same path
  2.

— concatenate the tokens, swap `▁` back to a space, and you recover the original text exactly. Classic BPE and WordPiece discard whitespace information (they pre-split on spaces) and need extra rules to detokenize

  Underneath, SentencePiece can run either BPE or a Unigram language model. T5 and LLaMA 1 / 2 both use it.

  <MyQuestion q="Is one of these methods better than the others? Which one do current LLMs use?">

, and the right choice depends on the use case. First, untangle three dimensions that often get lumped together:

    ```
    algorithm (how the vocabulary is learned)   BPE, WordPiece, Unigram LM
    base unit                                   characters / bytes (byte-level)
    tool / implementation                       SentencePiece, tiktoken, Hugging Face tokenizers
    ```

    SentencePiece isn't a third algorithm; it's a training framework that needs no pre-tokenization and runs BPE or Unigram inside. Unigram works in the opposite direction from BPE: start from a large candidate vocabulary and, each round, drop the tokens whose removal hurts corpus likelihood the least, until the target size is reached.

    | Method | Weakness it fixes | Limitation |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | BPE | Statistical merging solves OOV and vocabulary blow-up | Merges by raw frequency, so very common pieces can mislead it |
    | WordPiece | A correlation score merges more meaningful pieces | Still needs pre-tokenization; longest match can fall back to `[UNK]` |
    | SentencePiece (BPE / Unigram) | No reliance on spaces; handles CJK and mixed text uniformly; reversible | Doesn't define the merge criterion itself — results depend on the algorithm and corpus inside |

(per public information):

    ```
    GPT-4 / GPT-4o     byte-level BPE (tiktoken: cl100k_base / o200k_base)
    LLaMA 1 / 2        SentencePiece + BPE (32k, character-level + byte fallback)
    LLaMA 3            byte-level BPE (tiktoken-based, 128k)
    Gemma / Gemini     SentencePiece
    BERT               WordPiece
    T5                 SentencePiece + Unigram
    Claude             proprietary, unpublished; count tokens with the official token-counting API
    ```

    The trend is clear:

Byte-level guarantees any text can be encoded (see the byte-level BPE Q\&A under OOV below), and a large vocabulary fits the same text into fewer tokens.
  </MyQuestion>

  ### How do you choose a vocabulary size?

  A direct trade-off with no universal answer:

  | | Small vocab (e.g. 32k) | Large vocab (e.g. 200k) |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Embedding parameters | fewer, saves memory | many (`vocab_size × hidden_dim`, potentially hundreds of millions) |
  | Output softmax | fast | slow — probabilities over the whole vocabulary |
  | Tokens per passage | more, eats context | fewer, fits more into context |
  | Rare words / multilingual | shredded into pieces | well covered |

  Some real numbers for calibration:

  ```
  BERT-base      30,522
  LLaMA 1 / 2    32,000
  GPT-2          50,257
  cl100k_base    100,277   (GPT-4 / GPT-3.5-turbo)
  LLaMA 3        128,256
  o200k_base     200,019   (GPT-4o)
  ```

  The trend is clear:

A larger vocabulary compresses the same text into fewer tokens, which pays off more and more in the long-context era, while the extra embedding parameters are now negligible next to total model size.

  ### How are out-of-vocabulary words handled?

  With subword tokenization, OOV is largely a solved problem, but the full answer has three layers:

  1.

(the standard): unseen words decompose into known subwords, e.g. `"tokenization"` → `["token", "ization"]`, preserving most information
  2.
: GPT-family models use byte-level BPE, where the smallest unit is a
, not a character. Since any text can be represented as bytes,

— emoji, mojibake, and binary strings all encode
  3.

(legacy): drop it entirely and lose the information. Modern tokenizers rarely need this

  <MyQuestion q="How does byte-level BPE differ from regular BPE? How does it handle Chinese, and how do today's large vocabularies make Chinese cheaper?">

The merge algorithm is exactly the walkthrough above; what changes is what step 0 splits text into:

    | | Character-level BPE (regular) | Byte-level BPE |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Step 0 splits into | Unicode characters | UTF-8 bytes |
    | Starting set | whatever characters the corpus contains — thousands to tens of thousands,

|
    | An unseen character | OOV, becomes `[UNK]` | can't happen |
    | Cost | large starting set, still hits OOV | languages rare in the corpus get split into byte fragments |
    | Used by | early machine-translation BPE; LLaMA 1 / 2 (with byte fallback) | GPT models from GPT-2 on (tiktoken), LLaMA 3 |

The walkthrough used English, so step 0 had a dozen letters and the problem stayed hidden. But Unicode has about 150,000 characters and adds emoji every year, so no corpus covers them all. A rare character or a brand-new emoji has no slot even at step 0, so it becomes `[UNK]`. It's the word-level OOV problem again, one level down: smaller, not gone.

All text is stored as UTF-8 bytes, and a byte has only 256 possible values. Whatever new character shows up is still some combination of those 256, so "a base unit we've never seen" can't happen.

    Take `中` as an example:

    ```
    "A"   → 1 byte in UTF-8    0x41
    "中"  → 3 bytes in UTF-8   0xE4 0xB8 0xAD

    character-level:  中 is one unit at step 0
                      Chinese in the corpus → can keep merging with other characters
                      no Chinese at all     → 中 isn't in the vocabulary → [UNK]

    byte-level:       中 is three units at step 0: E4 / B8 / AD
                      Chinese in the corpus → the 3 bytes merge into 1 token
                      no Chinese at all     → stays as 3 byte fragments, but still encodes
    ```

: LLaMA 1 / 2 use character-level SentencePiece BPE, but the vocabulary also carries 256 byte tokens (`<0x00>` … `<0xFF>`). Known characters split as characters; only unknown ones fall back to bytes. So it never hits OOV either.

Efficiency comes down to two things, and that's exactly why large vocabularies help Chinese so much:

    1.

GPT-2 is 256 bytes + 50,000 merges. Merges go to the most frequent pairs; GPT-2's corpus was mostly English, so English pieces took most of the budget and plenty of Chinese characters ran out before their 3 bytes were merged. At 100k or 200k entries, the extra merges finally reach whole Chinese characters, even common words
    2.

The team chooses that corpus, and multilingual tokenizers usually raise the share of Chinese, Japanese, and so on on purpose. Frequent pieces get merged earlier. A bigger vocabulary trained on almost-all-English text would help Chinese much less

    Both effects together, measured with tiktoken:

    ```
                      "中国"                         a 70-character Chinese passage
    GPT-2   (50k)     3 tokens: 中 / E5 9B / BD      143 tokens (~2 per character)
    cl100k  (100k)    1 token                        82 tokens (~1.2 per character)
    o200k   (200k)    1 token                        50 tokens (~0.7 per character)
    ```

    In GPT-2, `中` already merged into a whole character while `国` stayed as two byte fragments: the more common a character, the earlier it gets a merge.

    A side effect you can actually see: when streaming, if a character is split across two tokens and the client doesn't buffer bytes, the first half can't be decoded yet and briefly shows up as `�`.

    For estimating Chinese token counts, and why "Chinese is always more expensive" is wrong, see Level 3 and Traps.
  </MyQuestion>

It matters because **every notion of "length" in an LLM is measured in tokens**, not characters:

  * positional encoding indexes token positions
  * KV cache memory grows with token count

  Tokenization is the exchange rate between a piece of text and a dollar amount.

  <MyQuestion q="What exactly are the input and output of tokenization? What are encode and decode, and is tokenization the same as encoding?">

python

    tokenizer.decode(ids)                     # "Hello, world!"

    input tokens    → read all at once during prefill
       ↓
    output tokens   → token ids the model generates one at a time during decode
       ↓ tokenizer decode (the lookup in reverse: id → string)
    the response text you see

  ### How do token, token id, and embedding relate?

  These get conflated constantly, but they're three distinct stages of a pipeline:

  | Stage | Output | Carries meaning? |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Tokenization | a **string fragment** like

  | Vocabulary lookup | an **integer id** like

| no — it's just a row number |
  | Embedding | a **vector** like

| yes — meaning starts here |

  The key point: **token ids carry no semantics**. Ids 1917 and 1918 are numerically adjacent but may represent totally unrelated words. Meaning is learned entirely by the embedding layer — a

matrix that the token id indexes into.

  <Note title="Why this distinction matters in interviews" type="tip">
    If you're asked "how does tokenization capture meaning," the correct answer is that it doesn't. Tokenization only splits and numbers; meaning is the job of embedding plus attention downstream. Getting this wrong signals shaky fundamentals.

  ### Why bill per token instead of per word or per character?

  Because the token is the model's real unit of compute. Each forward pass costs in proportion to the number of tokens in the sequence — regardless of whether a token is a five-letter English word or a single Chinese character.

  An intuition (measured with cl100k):

"the"          3 chars    1 word   1 token
  "strawberry"   10 chars   1 word   3 tokens   ["str", "aw", "berry"]
  "中国"          2 chars    1 word   1 token

Counting characters, the cost ratio would be 3 : 10 : 2; counting words, 1 : 1 : 1. The model's actual compute is 1 : 3 : 1. Neither lines up — only tokens do.

  <Note title="This also explains a classic failure" type="tip">
    "Why can't an LLM count the r's in strawberry?" Because the model never saw the ten characters
. It saw three integers standing for

. Letter-level information was destroyed at the tokenization step.

  ### What are the main approaches, and what do they trade off?

  Three families, all trading **vocabulary size** against **sequence length**:

  | Method | Example | Vocab size | Sequence length | Main problem |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Word-level |
| huge (100k+) | short | severe OOV: unseen words become

| moderate (30k–200k) | moderate | the standard choice, no fatal flaw |
  | Character-level |

| tiny (hundreds) | very long | sequences blow up attention's O(n²) cost |

  Subword won because it takes the good half of both: **frequent words stay whole (
is one token) while rare words break into meaningful pieces (

)**. No OOV, no sequence explosion.

  ### How does BPE work? Work it out by hand

  The whole idea in one sentence: **repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, until the vocabulary reaches its target size.**

  Say the training corpus contains only four words, with these counts:

l o w </w>          × 5
  l o w e r </w>      × 2
  n e w e s t </w>    × 6
  w i d e s t </w>    × 3

n e w es t </w>     × 6
  w i d es t </w>     × 3
is highest, so merge it into

n e w est </w>      × 6
  w i d est </w>      × 3

Continuing:

  | Round | Merged pair | New token | Corpus becomes |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 1 | (e, s) |

|

  Stop when the vocabulary hits its target size. The final vocabulary contains **learned** subword units like

.

  **At inference time nothing is counted.** The merge rules learned during training are simply replayed in the same order. So a tokenizer is fully deterministic: same text, same tokenizer, always the same split.

  <Note title="Why BPE handles unseen words">
    Given
, which never appeared in training, BPE doesn't emit

from existing merge rules. Almost no information is lost. That's the core advantage of subword over word-level.
  </Note>

  <MyQuestion q="How does the vocabulary relate to an algorithm like BPE, and what decides the vocabulary size?">
    **The vocabulary grows out of training step by step; it isn't designed first and then handed to the algorithm.** Look back at the walkthrough above:

Step 0    vocab = every single character   {l, o, w, e, r, n, s, t, i, d, </w>}
    Round 1   merge (e, s) → es                vocab + es
    Round 2   merge (es, t) → est              vocab + est
    Round 3   merge (est, </w>) → est</w>      vocab + est</w>
Every merge adds exactly one entry. So

aren't two independently designed pieces — they're two records of the same training run: one logs the merge order, the other lists every token that exists at the end, with its id.

    **Vocabulary size is a hyperparameter set before training** (the main one; pre-tokenization rules and special tokens are others). The algorithm keeps merging until it hits that number:

target vocabulary size (you choose it)
       ↓ determines
    how many merge rounds run
       ↓ determines
    which tokens exist, and how coarse or fine the splits are
A real example that adds up: GPT-2's vocabulary is 50,257 = 256 base bytes + 50,000 merges + 1 special token (

).

    In one line: **the algorithm is how to learn, the vocabulary size is the parameter you give it, and the vocabulary is what comes out** — method → parameter → output. That's one reason GPT-2 (50k) and LLaMA 3 (128k), both BPE-family tokenizers, split the same sentence into different numbers of tokens; their training corpora and pre-tokenization rules differ too (see Level 3). For how to pick the size, see "How do you choose a vocabulary size?" below.
  </MyQuestion>

  <MyQuestion q="How are merge rules actually used at inference? Once training produces a vocabulary, why not just split using the vocabulary?">
    **Because the vocabulary alone isn't enough — you also need the merge order.** The vocabulary only answers "which tokens are valid." A word often has several splits that are all valid, and an unordered set can't tell you which to pick. The **order (rank)** of the merge rules can.

    Here's how BPE applies the rules at inference:

    1. Break the word into base units (characters or bytes)
    2. Among all current adjacent pairs, find the one whose rule was **learned earliest** (lowest rank) — wherever it sits, not just the leftmost
    3. Merge it and go back to step 2, until no pair matches any rule

    A counterexample shows why the order is required. Say the rules, in learned order, are:

rule 1 (learned first): (b, c) → bc
    rule 2                : (a, b) → ab

merge by rank (correct)          merge the first match left to right (wrong)
    a b c a                          a b c a
    (a,b)=rule 2, (b,c)=rule 1       hits (a,b) first and merges it
    → merge (b,c) first              → ab c a
    a bc a, no rule applies, stop    no rule applies, stop
    ["a", "bc", "a"]                 ["ab", "c", "a"]

Every token in both results is in the vocabulary, yet the splits differ. Inference has to reproduce the split used in training; otherwise the model gets a token sequence it has barely seen, and quality drops. That rank order is what "replayed in the same order" above refers to.

    In one line: **the vocabulary answers "what counts as a valid token"; the merge order answers "when several merges are valid, which goes first."**
  </MyQuestion>

  ### How does WordPiece differ from BPE?

  The procedure is nearly identical. **Only the criterion for choosing which pair to merge differs:**

BPE:        pick the pair with the highest freq(u, v)
  WordPiece:  pick the pair with the highest freq(u, v) / (freq(u) × freq(v))

The denominator **penalizes combinations whose parts are already common on their own**.

  Concretely: suppose

— a tiny score — and concludes they merely happen to sit next to each other rather than forming a meaningful unit.

  Conversely, if
each occur only 10 times but 9 of those are together, WordPiece scores that very highly, because the parts are **strongly bound** and merging them into

is semantically justified.

  In one line: **BPE looks at raw frequency, WordPiece looks at correlation.**

① count every adjacent pair

    ④ repeat until the vocabulary hits its target size

  ### What problem does SentencePiece solve?

  Both methods above assume something: **first split the sentence into words by whitespace, then split subwords inside each word.** That assumption holds for English and fails completely for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, which have no spaces at all.

  SentencePiece's answer: **train directly on raw text and treat the space as just another character** (written

is that space. Two benefits follow:

  1. **No pre-tokenization needed** — mixed Chinese/English, Japanese, code, and messy social-media text all go through the same path
  2. **Fully reversible** — concatenate the tokens, swap

back to a space, and you recover the original text exactly. Classic BPE and WordPiece discard whitespace information (they pre-split on spaces) and need extra rules to detokenize

  Underneath, SentencePiece can run either BPE or a Unigram language model. T5 and LLaMA 1 / 2 both use it.

  <MyQuestion q="Is one of these methods better than the others? Which one do current LLMs use?">
    **It isn't a ranking — each one fixes a weakness of the one before**, and the right choice depends on the use case. First, untangle three dimensions that often get lumped together:

algorithm (how the vocabulary is learned)   BPE, WordPiece, Unigram LM
    base unit                                   characters / bytes (byte-level)
    tool / implementation                       SentencePiece, tiktoken, Hugging Face tokenizers

SentencePiece isn't a third algorithm; it's a training framework that needs no pre-tokenization and runs BPE or Unigram inside. Unigram works in the opposite direction from BPE: start from a large candidate vocabulary and, each round, drop the tokens whose removal hurts corpus likelihood the least, until the target size is reached.

    | Method | Weakness it fixes | Limitation |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | BPE | Statistical merging solves OOV and vocabulary blow-up | Merges by raw frequency, so very common pieces can mislead it |
    | WordPiece | A correlation score merges more meaningful pieces | Still needs pre-tokenization; longest match can fall back to

|
    | SentencePiece (BPE / Unigram) | No reliance on spaces; handles CJK and mixed text uniformly; reversible | Doesn't define the merge criterion itself — results depend on the algorithm and corpus inside |

    **What major models use** (per public information):

GPT-4 / GPT-4o     byte-level BPE (tiktoken: cl100k_base / o200k_base)
    LLaMA 1 / 2        SentencePiece + BPE (32k, character-level + byte fallback)
    LLaMA 3            byte-level BPE (tiktoken-based, 128k)
    Gemma / Gemini     SentencePiece
    BERT               WordPiece
    T5                 SentencePiece + Unigram
    Claude             proprietary, unpublished; count tokens with the official token-counting API

The trend is clear: **recent LLMs have largely converged on byte-level BPE with large vocabularies.** Byte-level guarantees any text can be encoded (see the byte-level BPE Q\&A under OOV below), and a large vocabulary fits the same text into fewer tokens.
  </MyQuestion>

  ### How do you choose a vocabulary size?

  A direct trade-off with no universal answer:

  | | Small vocab (e.g. 32k) | Large vocab (e.g. 200k) |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Embedding parameters | fewer, saves memory | many (

, potentially hundreds of millions) |
  | Output softmax | fast | slow — probabilities over the whole vocabulary |
  | Tokens per passage | more, eats context | fewer, fits more into context |
  | Rare words / multilingual | shredded into pieces | well covered |

  Some real numbers for calibration:

BERT-base      30,522
  LLaMA 1 / 2    32,000
  GPT-2          50,257
  cl100k_base    100,277   (GPT-4 / GPT-3.5-turbo)
  LLaMA 3        128,256
  o200k_base     200,019   (GPT-4o)

The trend is clear: **vocabularies are growing.** A larger vocabulary compresses the same text into fewer tokens, which pays off more and more in the long-context era, while the extra embedding parameters are now negligible next to total model size.

  ### How are out-of-vocabulary words handled?

  With subword tokenization, OOV is largely a solved problem, but the full answer has three layers:

  1. **Subword splitting** (the standard): unseen words decompose into known subwords, e.g.

, preserving most information
  2. **Byte-level fallback**: GPT-family models use byte-level BPE, where the smallest unit is a **byte**, not a character. Since any text can be represented as bytes, **OOV is impossible in principle** — emoji, mojibake, and binary strings all encode
  3. **An

token** (legacy): drop it entirely and lose the information. Modern tokenizers rarely need this

  <MyQuestion q="How does byte-level BPE differ from regular BPE? How does it handle Chinese, and how do today's large vocabularies make Chinese cheaper?">
    **Only one thing differs: the unit merging starts from.** The merge algorithm is exactly the walkthrough above; what changes is what step 0 splits text into:

    | | Character-level BPE (regular) | Byte-level BPE |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Step 0 splits into | Unicode characters | UTF-8 bytes |
    | Starting set | whatever characters the corpus contains — thousands to tens of thousands, **open-ended** | always 256, **closed** |
    | An unseen character | OOV, becomes

| can't happen |
    | Cost | large starting set, still hits OOV | languages rare in the corpus get split into byte fragments |
    | Used by | early machine-translation BPE; LLaMA 1 / 2 (with byte fallback) | GPT models from GPT-2 on (tiktoken), LLaMA 3 |

    **Why does character-level still hit OOV?** The walkthrough used English, so step 0 had a dozen letters and the problem stayed hidden. But Unicode has about 150,000 characters and adds emoji every year, so no corpus covers them all. A rare character or a brand-new emoji has no slot even at step 0, so it becomes

. It's the word-level OOV problem again, one level down: smaller, not gone.

    **Why do bytes fix it?** All text is stored as UTF-8 bytes, and a byte has only 256 possible values. Whatever new character shows up is still some combination of those 256, so "a base unit we've never seen" can't happen.

    Take

"A"   → 1 byte in UTF-8    0x41
    "中"  → 3 bytes in UTF-8   0xE4 0xB8 0xAD

    character-level:  中 is one unit at step 0
                      Chinese in the corpus → can keep merging with other characters
                      no Chinese at all     → 中 isn't in the vocabulary → [UNK]

    byte-level:       中 is three units at step 0: E4 / B8 / AD
                      Chinese in the corpus → the 3 bytes merge into 1 token
                      no Chinese at all     → stays as 3 byte fragments, but still encodes
**The middle ground, byte fallback**: LLaMA 1 / 2 use character-level SentencePiece BPE, but the vocabulary also carries 256 byte tokens (

). Known characters split as characters; only unknown ones fall back to bytes. So it never hits OOV either.

    **Byte-level guarantees text can be encoded, not that it's encoded efficiently.** Efficiency comes down to two things, and that's exactly why large vocabularies help Chinese so much:

    1. **A bigger vocabulary means more merge rounds.** GPT-2 is 256 bytes + 50,000 merges. Merges go to the most frequent pairs; GPT-2's corpus was mostly English, so English pieces took most of the budget and plenty of Chinese characters ran out before their 3 bytes were merged. At 100k or 200k entries, the extra merges finally reach whole Chinese characters, even common words
    2. **More Chinese in the tokenizer's training corpus.** The team chooses that corpus, and multilingual tokenizers usually raise the share of Chinese, Japanese, and so on on purpose. Frequent pieces get merged earlier. A bigger vocabulary trained on almost-all-English text would help Chinese much less

    Both effects together, measured with tiktoken:

"中国"                         a 70-character Chinese passage
    GPT-2   (50k)     3 tokens: 中 / E5 9B / BD      143 tokens (~2 per character)
    cl100k  (100k)    1 token                        82 tokens (~1.2 per character)
    o200k   (200k)    1 token                        50 tokens (~0.7 per character)
already merged into a whole character while

stayed as two byte fragments: the more common a character, the earlier it gets a merge.

    A side effect you can actually see: when streaming, if a character is split across two tokens and the client doesn't buffer bytes, the first half can't be decoded yet and briefly shows up as

  ### How does token count propagate into latency and cost?

  This chain is the single most important thing on this page:
</Locale>

<Locale lang="zh">
  拆开说：

  * **Prefill 阶段**：模型要一次性处理完整个 prompt。这部分可以并行，但 attention 里的

是 n×n 的矩阵，所以计算量随 n 平方增长。prompt 越长，首 token 出来得越慢（TTFT 越高）
  * **KV Cache**：每个 token 都要缓存它的 K 和 V 向量，显存占用随 n **线性**增长。显存被吃满，单卡能同时跑的请求数就下降，摊到每个请求的成本就上升
  * **Context Window**：装不下就必须截断或压缩，这时候才需要 [Context Engineering](/docs/context) 那一整套东西

  ### 为什么 output token 比 input token 贵好几倍？

  因为两者的计算方式根本不同：

Input token  → Prefill  → 一次性并行处理完 → 单位成本低
  Output token → Decode   → 一次只能生成 1 个 → 无法并行 → 单位成本高

生成 100 个 output token，意味着要跑 100 次前向传播，每次都要重新读一遍全部模型权重。而 100 个 input token 只需要 1 次前向传播就全处理完了。

  **工程结论：想省钱和降延迟，先砍 output 长度，再砍 input 长度。** 一个「请简短回答」的指令，省下来的钱通常比压缩 prompt 更多。

  <Note title="这也解释了 prompt caching 为什么有用" type="tip">
    既然 prefill 的成本来自「重新处理一遍 prompt」，那把不变的前缀（system prompt、few-shot 例子）缓存下来，就能直接跳过这部分计算。这就是 [Caching](/docs/context/caching) 的原理。
  </Note>

  <MyQuestion q="为什么 output token 只能一个一个生成？不能像 input 那样并行，或者一次生成好几个吗？">
    **关键区别：input 是已经存在的，output 是还不存在的。**

    * **Prefill**：你发出请求时，prompt 里每个 token 都已经确定。模型可以把它们放进一次前向计算，所有位置并行算完（causal mask 保证每个位置只看它前面的 token）
    * **Decode**：LLM 是自回归模型，生成第 k 个 token 时，输入必须包含第 1 … k−1 个 token 的**真实结果**：

生成第 1 个：看 [prompt]
    生成第 2 个：看 [prompt] + 第 1 个     ← 第 1 个要先算完、采样出来才存在
    生成第 3 个：看 [prompt] + 第 1、2 个

这是严格的先后依赖：不是「数据都在、只是还没算」，而是下一步的输入要等上一步采样完才出现。

    **为什么不能一次猜好几个？** 可以猜，但第 5 个 token 就得建立在「假设的」第 2–4 个上。如果第 3 个实际采样出 "dog"，而你假设的是 "cat"，第 5 个就接不上了。所以标准 decode 必须串行。

    工程上有两种「绕开」的办法，都不违反这个依赖：

    * **跨请求并行**：同一时刻把很多用户的 decode 拼进一个 batch（continuous batching），但每条序列仍然一步只前进一个 token
    * **Speculative decoding**：让一个小模型先草拟几个 token，大模型用**一次**前向计算并行验证，从第一个不对的位置丢弃重来。猜中得越多越省时间，而且输出分布和逐个生成完全一样

    细节见 [Inference](/docs/llm/inference)。
  </MyQuestion>

  ### 为什么同一段文本在不同模型上 token 数不同？

  因为**每个模型有自己的 tokenizer 和词表**，而且 tokenizer 是和模型权重一起训练 / 发布的，不能混用。

  这意味着一个很实际的工程陷阱：

  > 你在 GPT-4 上测出某个 prompt 是 1200 token，换到另一个模型上，它可能是 950 或 1400 token。**拿旧的 token 数 × 新的单价，算出来的成本是错的。**

  做跨模型成本对比时，必须用**各自的 tokenizer 重新数一遍**。

  ### 中文 / 代码场景怎么估算 token？

  不要背固定比例，**要实测**：同一段中文换个 tokenizer，token 数能差将近 3 倍（实测见 Level 2 byte-level BPE 那条问答）。粗略的量感：

英文     ≈ 1 token / 0.75 词    （约 4 个字符 1 个 token）
  中文     cl100k 每字约 1.2 个 token，o200k 每字约 0.7 个
  代码     缩进、符号很吃 token，通常比同长度英文散文贵

python
# OpenAI
import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4o")
print(len(enc.encode("your text")))

# open models on HuggingFace
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-3-8B")
print(len(tok.encode("your text")))

<Locale lang="en">
  <Note title="Direct consequence for RAG" type="tip">
    Chunk size must be defined in **tokens**, not characters. The same "500" applied to Chinese versus English can differ by 2x in actual tokens, throwing off your context budget. See [Chunking](/docs/rag/chunking).
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note title="A token is not a word, and not a character either" type="warning">
    A token can be a whole word, a subword, a single character, punctuation, or even a **leading space** —

are two different tokens in most tokenizers. Saying "one Chinese character equals one token" invites an immediate follow-up.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Don't claim Chinese is always more expensive" type="danger">
    That's an outdated conclusion. The small vocabularies of the GPT-2 / GPT-3 era handled Chinese badly, about 2 tokens per character on average; with o200k the same passage takes about 0.7. The accurate framing: **token efficiency depends on vocabulary size and on how well that language is represented in the tokenizer's training corpus.** Measure, don't recite.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Latency doesn't scale linearly with total tokens" type="warning">
    Input goes through prefill and parallelizes; output goes through decode and doesn't. Latency is driven mainly by **output length**, not total token count. "Longer prompts are slower" is only half true.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Tokenization produces no semantics" type="warning">
    Its output is an **integer id** — purely a lookup row number. Meaning appears at the embedding layer. Asked "how does tokenization understand meaning," the right answer is that it doesn't.
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Connections
</Locale>

Tokenization
   ↓
Vocabulary ──→ Embedding ──→ Context Window
   ↓                              ↓
per-token billing           Prefill / KV Cache
   ↓                              ↓
Cost ←──────────────────────  Latency

title: Attention & Transformer
description: 从 Encoder / Decoder 讲起，一步步搭出 attention、Transformer 和今天的 LLM，再落到 KV cache 和长上下文成本。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Every LLM today is built on the Transformer, and the heart of the Transformer is attention. Interview questions like "why is long context expensive," "what does the KV cache store," and "why is everyone decoder-only" all trace back to these two things.

  This page doesn't assume you've studied deep learning. It starts with a few math building blocks, explains what problem attention was invented to solve, assembles the parts into a Transformer step by step, and only then covers modern LLM improvements and engineering impact. **Every section uses only what came before it**, so skipping ahead makes things hard to follow.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Foundations | What are dot products, linear layers, softmax, tensor shapes, and training? | 20 min |
  | 1 · Encoders and decoders | Before attention, how did models handle a sentence, and what went wrong? | 30 min |
  | 2 · The intuition behind attention | How does attention fix "squeezing a sentence into one vector loses information"? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Self-attention | How do words in a sentence look at each other, and how exactly is it computed? | 45 min |
  | 4 · Three fixes | What gaps do multi-head attention, positional encoding, and masks each fill? | 45 min |
  | 5 · Assembling the Transformer | What's inside a block, and how does the original Transformer translate a sentence? | 45 min |
  | 6 · Three architectures | How do encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder differ, and why are LLMs decoder-only? | 30 min |
  | 7 · Modern LLM upgrades | What did models like LLaMA change from the original design, and why? | 45 min |
  | 8 · Engineering impact | How do O(n²), the KV cache, GQA, memory, and long-context cost work out? | 45 min |

  Each Level ends with a few self-check questions — **if you can't answer them, don't move on yet**. The whole page takes about 6 hours spread over several sessions; `/drill` remembers where you stopped.

  One example runs through the entire page: **translating 「我 爱 猫」 into "I love cats."** When we get to decoder-only models, it's the same sentence, just continued instead of translated.

  ## Must know

  * what dot products, linear layers, softmax, and the tensor shape `[batch, seq_len, d_model]` mean
  * what an encoder and a decoder are, and the two weaknesses of the RNN version
  * the intuition behind attention: Q / K / V, score → softmax → weighted average
  * the full self-attention computation, and why scores are divided by √d\_k
  * multi-head attention, positional encoding, the padding mask and the causal mask
  * the four parts of a Transformer block: attention, FFN, residual connections, LayerNorm
  * encoder-only vs. decoder-only vs. encoder-decoder, and why LLMs are decoder-only
  * modern upgrades: Pre-LN, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE and length extrapolation
  * engineering impact: parameters and memory, O(n²), the KV cache, MHA / MQA / GQA, long-context cost
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Foundations

  These are the building blocks every later section relies on. If you already know them, jump to the self-check at the end; if you can answer everything, skip ahead to Level 1.

  ### Vectors and dot products: how do numbers express "how similar are these two things"?

  **A vector is just a list of numbers.** As covered in [Tokenization](/docs/llm/tokenization), every token eventually becomes a vector (its embedding), and those numbers encode what the word means.

  **Dot product**: multiply matching positions of two vectors, then add everything up.

  ```
  [1, 2] · [2, 1] = 1×2 + 2×1 = 4
  ```

  The intuition: **the closer the directions, the larger the result.**

  ```
  [1, 2] · [ 2,  1] =  4     similar direction → positive, fairly large
  [1, 2] · [ 2, -1] =  0     perpendicular → 0, unrelated
  [1, 2] · [-1, -2] = -5     opposite direction → negative
  ```

  Now apply it to words. Suppose two numbers describe a word's meaning (the first means "animal-like," the second "machine-like"):

  ```
  cat = [0.9, 0.1]
  dog = [0.8, 0.2]
  car = [0.1, 0.9]

  cat · dog = 0.9×0.8 + 0.1×0.2 = 0.74    similar
  cat · car = 0.9×0.1 + 0.1×0.9 = 0.18    not similar
  ```

  **That's all you need to remember: the dot product is how a model measures how related two vectors are.** The "scoring" step in attention is exactly a dot product.

  <Note title="Dot products also react to magnitude">
    Keep the direction the same, make the numbers bigger, and the dot product grows. `[2, 4] · [4, 2] = 16`, four times `[1, 2] · [2, 1]`, even though the directions are identical. Dividing by √d\_k in Level 3 exists to deal with exactly this.
  </Note>

  ### Matrix multiplication: why is a "linear layer" just one matrix multiply?

  **A matrix is a table of numbers** with shape `[rows, columns]`. To compute `W · x`: **each number in the output is one row of W dotted with x.**

  ```
  W = [[1,  1],        x = [3, 1]
       [1, -1]]

  W · x = [ row 1 · x,          row 2 · x          ]
        = [ 1×3 + 1×1,          1×3 + (-1)×1       ]
        = [ 4, 2 ]
  ```

  So one matrix multiply is **a batch of dot products** that turns a vector into a different representation. That's exactly what a **linear layer** in a neural network does (usually plus a bias vector b):

  ```
  linear layer:  y = W · x + b
  shape rule:    W is [output dim, input dim]
                 a W of shape [2, 3] turns a 3-dim vector into a 2-dim one
  ```

  Two key takeaways:

  * **A neural network's "parameters" are mostly the numbers inside these W and b**, and "learning" means adjusting them
  * **Many tokens can be processed at once**: stack n token vectors into an `[n, d]` matrix and multiply by the same W, so every token is transformed by the same rule. W\_Q, W\_K, and W\_V in Level 3 are three linear layers like this

  ### Softmax: how do you turn a set of scores into probabilities?

  Models often score a set of candidates and then need those scores as probabilities that add up to 1. That step is softmax:

  ```
  softmax(xᵢ) = e^xᵢ / (e^x₁ + e^x₂ + … + e^xₙ)
  ```

  By hand for the scores `[2.0, 1.0, 0.1]`:

  ```
  e^2.0 = 7.389    e^1.0 = 2.718    e^0.1 = 1.105    total = 11.212

  softmax = [7.389 / 11.212,  2.718 / 11.212,  1.105 / 11.212]
          = [0.659, 0.242, 0.099]
  ```

  Three properties:

  1. **Every value is positive** (e raised to any power is above 0)
  2. **They add up to 1**, so they work as probabilities or weights
  3. **The order is preserved but the gaps get amplified**: a raw score of 2.0 is only twice 1.0, yet after softmax 0.659 is 2.7 times 0.242

  It shows up in two places later: turning attention scores into weights (Levels 2 and 3), and producing the model's probabilities for the next token (Level 6).

  ### How do you read tensor shapes? What does `[batch, seq_len, d_model]` mean?

  **A tensor is a multi-dimensional array**, and its shape lists how long each dimension is:

  ```
  scalar      5                                   shape []
  vector      [0.2, 0.7, 0.1]                     shape [3]
  matrix      3 tokens × 4 dims each              shape [3, 4]
  3D tensor   2 sentences × 5 tokens × 768 dims   shape [2, 5, 768]
  ```

  In LLMs the most common one is that last form, `[batch, seq_len, d_model]`:

  | Dimension | Value in the example | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | batch | 2 | how many sentences go in at once; computing them together lets the GPU parallelize, and sentences don't affect each other |
  | seq\_len | 5 | how many tokens each sentence has |
  | d\_model | 768 | how many numbers make up each token's vector (the model's "width") |

  Here's how the shape changes over the first steps:

  ```
  token ids          [2, 5]         integers from the tokenizer, not vectors yet
  after embedding    [2, 5, 768]    each id becomes a 768-dim vector
  ```

  What if the two sentences have different lengths? Pad the shorter one with `<pad>` so both fit in one tensor. The padding mask in Level 4 exists specifically to handle those filler positions.

  <Note title="Write the shape at every step when you draw it in an interview" type="tip">
    When explaining a Transformer, labeling how `[batch, seq_len, d_model]` changes beside each arrow is the most direct proof that you really understand the data flow. Every later section marks shapes — write them down as you read.
  </Note>

  ### What does "training" actually do? What are loss and gradients?

  The parameters — all the numbers in every W — start out random. Training repeats these four steps:

  ```
  ① forward pass       feed the input through the model and get a prediction, e.g. P(next word = "cats") = 0.2
  ② compute the loss   one number measuring how wrong the prediction is
  ③ compute gradients  for every parameter, which direction to nudge it so the loss drops (backpropagation)
  ④ update             move every parameter a small step in that direction

  back to ①, repeated millions to trillions of times
  ```

  **A loss example**: for next-token prediction, the usual loss is the negative log of the probability given to the correct answer:

  ```
  P(correct answer "cats") = 0.2  →  loss = -ln 0.2 = 1.609    quite wrong
  P(correct answer "cats") = 0.5  →  loss = -ln 0.5 = 0.693
  P(correct answer "cats") = 0.9  →  loss = -ln 0.9 = 0.105    nearly right
  ```

  **Gradients flow backward from the last layer toward the first**, getting multiplied by some factors at every layer along the way. With many layers, if those factors are usually below 1, the gradient is close to zero by the time it reaches the early layers, and those parameters barely learn. **That's what people mean when they say a deep network "won't train"** — the residual connections in Level 5 exist to fix it.

  <Note title="LLM pretraining is these four steps taken to the extreme">
    Across a huge amount of text, the model predicts the next token at every position and updates its parameters with the loss above, over and over. How it's trained and on how much data is on [Training](/docs/llm/training); for this page you only need "parameters are tuned during training," "loss measures how wrong," and "if gradients can't flow back, the network won't train."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: by now you should be able to answer">
    1. What's the dot product of `[1, 0]` and `[0, 1]`, and what does that tell you?
    2. A W of shape `[64, 768]` turns a 768-dim vector into how many dimensions?
    3. What is `softmax([0, 0, 0])`?
    4. In the tensor `[8, 100, 4096]`, what does each number mean?
    5. What situation does "won't train" usually describe?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Where the problem comes from: encoders and decoders

  Attention didn't appear out of nowhere — it was invented to patch a specific design flaw. Once you see that flaw clearly, every later improvement makes sense.

  ### What is a sequence task, and why can't an ordinary neural network handle it?

  A sequence task is one where the input or output is an ordered series of items:

  | Task | Input | Output | Example |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Translation | a series of words | another series of words | 「我 爱 猫」→ "I love cats" |
  | Continuation | a series of words | the next word | "I love" → "cats" |
  | Classification | a series of words | one label | "This place is amazing" → positive |

  An ordinary network built from the linear layers in Level 0 can't handle this, for two reasons:

  1. **The input size has to be fixed**: W's shape is set in stone, but sentences vary in length
  2. **Order matters**: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" use the same words with opposite meanings

  So we need a model that **handles any length and reads in order**. Before Transformers, the standard answer was the RNN.

  ### How does an RNN read a sentence one word at a time?

  The core of an RNN (recurrent neural network) is a "memory" vector called the **hidden state** h. Each time it reads a word, it combines the old memory with the new word to produce a new memory:

  ```
  h_t = tanh( W_h · h_(t-1)  +  W_x · x_t )
              ↑ old memory        ↑ vector for the current word
  ```

  `tanh` is a function that **squashes any number into the range -1 to 1**, so values don't keep growing.

  Let's work it through. To keep it hand-computable, simplify the parameters: W\_h means "multiply each number by 0.5," W\_x means "leave it unchanged," the word vectors are `我 = [1, 0]`, `爱 = [0, 1]`, `猫 = [1, 1]`, and the starting memory is `h₀ = [0, 0]`:

  ```
  read 我:  h₁ = tanh( 0.5 × [0, 0]         + [1, 0] ) = tanh([1.000, 0.000]) = [0.762, 0.000]
  read 爱:  h₂ = tanh( 0.5 × [0.762, 0]     + [0, 1] ) = tanh([0.381, 1.000]) = [0.363, 0.762]
  read 猫:  h₃ = tanh( 0.5 × [0.363, 0.762] + [1, 1] ) = tanh([1.182, 1.381]) = [0.828, 0.881]
  ```

  After the whole sentence, `h₃ = [0.828, 0.881]` is everything the model "understands" about 「我 爱 猫」.

  ### What is an encoder, and what is a decoder?

  Translation splits naturally into two roles:

  * **The encoder reads**: it goes through the input sentence start to finish and turns it into vectors that capture what the sentence means
  * **The decoder writes**: it takes the encoder's representation and generates the output one word at a time

  Translation with RNNs looks like this:

  ```
  Encoder reads the source
    我  →  h₁
    爱  →  h₂
    猫  →  h₃   ← done. h₃ goes to the decoder as "the meaning of the sentence," often called the context vector c

  Decoder writes the translation (carrying c at every step)
    input <bos>   →  output I
    input I       →  output love
    input love    →  output cats
    input cats    →  output <eos>    ← generation ends
  ```

  `<bos>` and `<eos>` are special tokens marking the beginning and end.

  Notice one key property of the decoder: **at every step, the word it generated last becomes this step's input**. Generating by feeding your own output back in is called **autoregressive** generation — and it's exactly how today's LLMs emit tokens one at a time.

  An analogy: an encoder-decoder works like a consecutive interpreter who listens to the whole sentence first, then speaks the translation word by word.

  <Note title="Encoder and decoder are roles, not specific structures">
    Here they're built with RNNs; in Level 5 they'll be built from Transformer blocks, but the split — one reads, one writes — stays the same. So when Level 6 talks about encoder-only and decoder-only models, it means "keep only the reading half" and "keep only the writing half."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Don't confuse the model's encoder with the tokenizer's encode" type="warning">
    Both are called "encode," but they live at completely different levels:

    ```
    text → tokenizer.encode → token ids → embedding → Encoder → contextual representation
           ↑ a lookup, no neural network               ↑ a neural network module
    ```

    `tokenizer.encode` is the "text → integer ids" step from [Tokenization](/docs/llm/tokenization); the Encoder inside a model is a neural network that reads vectors and produces contextual representations. Mixing them up in an interview comes across as fuzzy on the concepts.
  </Note>

  ### What's wrong with this design?

  **Weakness ①: an information bottleneck.** Whether the source is 3 words or 300, the decoder receives one fixed-length vector, h₃ (2 dims above; hundreds to thousands in real models). The longer the sentence, the more the earliest words get washed out.

  Try an experiment with the toy RNN above: swap the first word 我 for 你 (vector `[-1, 0]`), keep everything else the same, and see how much the final h changes:

  ```
  3-word sentence     final h differs by 0.154
  5-word sentence     final h differs by 0.011
  10-word sentence    identical to 4 decimal places
  ```

  By the 10th word the model has "forgotten" whether the first word was 我 or 你. The reason is simple: every new word multiplies the old memory by 0.5 and squashes it through tanh again, so the first word's influence gets diluted layer after layer. Real RNNs learn their parameters, and LSTMs and GRUs add "gates" to reduce forgetting, but **the bottleneck of squeezing the whole sentence into one vector never goes away**.

  **Weakness ②: no parallelism.** Computing h₃ has to wait for h₂, which has to wait for h₁. A 1,000-token sentence means 1,000 sequential steps. GPUs are built to compute huge amounts at once, yet here they sit waiting step by step, so training is slow and models are hard to scale.

  <Note title="Keep these two problems in mind as you read on" type="tip">
    The next two Levels fix them one at a time: **attention in Level 2 fixes ①** (the decoder no longer depends on a single vector), and **self-attention in Level 3 fixes ②** (the RNN's step-by-step computation goes away entirely). Put the two fixes together and you have the Transformer.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: by now you should be able to answer">
    1. What is an RNN's hidden state, and why is it called "memory"?
    2. In translation, what is the encoder responsible for, and what is the decoder responsible for?
    3. What does autoregressive mean, and where does it show up in today's LLMs?
    4. How is the tokenizer's encode different from the Encoder inside a model?
    5. What are the two weaknesses of an RNN encoder-decoder?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · The intuition behind attention

  ### When translating each word, where in the source should the model look?

  When a person translates into "I love cats," writing "love" sends their eyes back to 爱 in the source, and writing "cats" sends them back to 猫:

  ```
  I     ↔  我
  love  ↔  爱
  cats  ↔  猫
  ```

  The Level 1 design can't do this: the decoder holds only h₃, and where each source word was and what it said have long since blurred together.

  Attention's idea is simple: **don't hand the decoder only the final h₃ — keep every encoder step, h₁, h₂, and h₃.** Each time the decoder generates a word, it looks back and takes what it needs from all three: more from whatever is most relevant right now, less from the rest.

  The idea was proposed for translation models in 2014 (often called Bahdanau attention), and it's the starting point for every form of attention since.

  ### What are Q, K, and V, and what does "take what it needs" mean?

  Start with an ordinary dictionary lookup. A Python dict:

  ```python
  d = {"我": content1, "爱": content2, "猫": content3}
  d["爱"]   # the key must match exactly, and you get back exactly one entry
  ```

  Attention is a **soft lookup**: take a question, compare it with **every** key, then return **all** the values blended by similarity. Three roles:

  | Role | In a dictionary lookup | In translation |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | **Query (Q)** | the question you look up | the decoder's current state: "I'm about to write the next word — what do I need?" |
  | **Key (K)** | each entry's label, used for matching | each source position's label: "here's what I have" |
  | **Value (V)** | each entry's actual content | the content that gets taken from each source position |

  In this earliest translation version, **K and V are both the encoder's h₁, h₂, h₃** (the same thing used two ways), and Q is the decoder's current state. Similarity is the dot product from Level 0.

  <Note title="Why separate the label from the content?">
    The information used to judge relevance and the information you actually want to take aren't necessarily the same. In a library you find a book by its title and call number (the key), but what you carry away is the book's content (the value). Here they're identical for now; Level 3 gives K and V their own linear layers so the model can learn to separate them.
  </Note>

  ### Walk through it: how is attention computed when generating "love"?

  To keep the math easy, keys are 3-dim and values are 2-dim:

  ```
  source   Key (label)       Value (content)
  我       k = [1, 0, 0]     v = [1.0, 0.0]
  爱       k = [0, 1, 0]     v = [0.0, 1.0]
  猫       k = [0, 0, 1]     v = [0.5, 0.5]

  decoder's query when it's about to generate "love":  q = [0.1, 2.0, 0.3]
  ```

  **Step 1: score** — dot the query with every key

  ```
  q · k我 = 0.1×1 + 2.0×0 + 0.3×0 = 0.1
  q · k爱 = 0.1×0 + 2.0×1 + 0.3×0 = 2.0
  q · k猫 = 0.1×0 + 2.0×0 + 0.3×1 = 0.3
  ```

  **Step 2: softmax** — turn the scores into weights that add up to 1

  ```
  softmax([0.1, 2.0, 0.3]) = [0.112, 0.751, 0.137]
  ```

  **Step 3: weighted average** — blend the values using those weights

  ```
  0.112 × [1.0, 0.0] + 0.751 × [0.0, 1.0] + 0.137 × [0.5, 0.5]
  = [0.112 + 0.069,  0.751 + 0.069]
  = [0.181, 0.819]
  ```

  The result, `[0.181, 0.819]`, is called the **context vector**, and 75% of it comes from 爱. The decoder combines it with its own state to decide that this step's output is "love."

  **Every generated word has a different query, so the weights change too.** All three steps worked out:

  ```
  generating   looks at 我   looks at 爱   looks at 猫
  I            0.761         0.126         0.114
  love         0.112         0.751         0.137
  cats         0.126         0.114         0.761
  ```

  This table is called the **alignment matrix**. Each row sums to 1, and the largest weights fall right on the diagonal — the model has "aligned" source and translation.

  <Note title="In a real model, nobody sets the queries and keys">
    The numbers above were chosen to be easy to compute. In a real model, q and k are computed by the network, and its parameters are learned. During training the model discovers that "looking at 爱 when generating love makes the prediction more accurate and the loss lower," so it learns on its own to make that dot product the largest. Also, Bahdanau's original version scored with a small neural network (called additive attention); the Transformer switched to the faster dot product.
  </Note>

  ### What did attention fix, and what's still unfixed?

  **It fixed weakness ① (the information bottleneck).** The decoder no longer depends on a single h₃; at every step it sees every source position directly. Even a 300-word source doesn't have to be crammed into one vector, and the first word is just as "close" to the decoder as the last.

  **It didn't fix weakness ② (no parallelism).** The encoder and decoder are still RNNs, so h₃ still waits for h₂.

  This kind of attention, where **Q comes from the decoder and K and V come from the encoder**, is called **cross-attention**: two different sequences looking at each other. Remember the name — it comes back in Level 5 when we assemble the original Transformer.

  <Note title="The key idea for what comes next" type="tip">
    If attention lets the decoder look at every encoder position, **why not let the words in a sentence look at each other directly, with no RNN at all?** Every word would get the whole sentence's context, and nothing would have to wait. That's self-attention in Level 3 — and what the 2017 Transformer paper's title, "Attention Is All You Need," means.
  </Note>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Self-attention: letting the words in a sentence look at each other

  ### How do you apply attention to a sentence itself?

  In Level 2, Q came from the decoder and K and V came from the encoder — two sequences looking at each other. Self-attention moves this **inside a single sequence**: every word in the sentence acts as the Q that asks, the K that gets matched, and the V that gets taken.

  Why do that? Because a word's embedding on its own is fixed, while meaning depends on context:

  ```
  "I sat by the river bank."        → bank ≈ riverside
  "I deposited money at the bank."  → bank ≈ financial institution
  ```

  Self-attention lets "bank" look at every word in the sentence. In the first one it finds "river" highly relevant and pulls in more from it; in the second it pulls more from "money." The same word ends up with two different new vectors.

  In our running example, 爱 looks at 我 and 猫 to learn who loves whom, and 猫 looks at 爱 to learn it's the one being loved. **After reading the whole sentence, every word becomes a context-aware version of itself** — exactly what the RNN in Level 1 tried to do with its hidden state and did poorly.

  ### Where do Q, K, and V come from when they all start from the same input?

  In Level 2, K and V were simply the encoder's h — the same thing. Self-attention gives each of the three roles **its own linear layer** (the `W · x` from Level 0):

  ```
  Q = X · W_Q
  K = X · W_K
  V = X · W_V
  ```

  * X: the input, shape `[n, d_model]`, one row per token
  * W\_Q, W\_K, W\_V: three learnable matrices, trained once and fixed at inference
  * each token's vector is multiplied by all three to get its own q, k, and v

  Why project the same word into three different vectors? Because they're three different jobs:

  | Projection | Question it answers | Library analogy |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Q | What information am I looking for? | your search request |
  | K | How can others find me? | the title and call number |
  | V | What do I hand over once found? | the book's content |

  With three separate sets of parameters, the model learns for itself both "what counts as relevant" and "what to take once something is relevant" — far more flexible than dotting X with X directly. **"What counts as similar" isn't defined by a person; the model learns it by learning these three matrices.**

  ### Work it by hand: self-attention on 「我 爱 猫」

  Use the word vectors from Level 1 as input, with d\_model = d\_k = 2:

  ```
  X:  我 = [1, 0]    爱 = [0, 1]    猫 = [1, 1]

  Simple values to keep the math easy (W_K is the identity, so K equals X):
  W_Q = [[1, 0],     W_K = [[1, 0],     W_V = [[2, 0],
         [1, 2]]            [0, 1]]            [0, 1]]
  ```

  **Step 0: project.** Multiply each token's row vector by the three matrices:

  ```
          Q = X · W_Q     K = X · W_K     V = X · W_V
  我      [1, 0]          [1, 0]          [2, 0]
  爱      [1, 2]          [0, 1]          [0, 1]
  猫      [2, 2]          [1, 1]          [2, 1]
  ```

  For example, 爱's Q is `[0, 1] · W_Q`, which picks out W\_Q's second row: `[1, 2]`.

  **Step 1: score.** Dot every word's q with every word's k, giving a 3 × 3 table:

  ```
                 looks at 我 k=[1,0]   looks at 爱 k=[0,1]   looks at 猫 k=[1,1]
  我 q=[1,0]           1                     0                     1
  爱 q=[1,2]           1                     2                     3
  猫 q=[2,2]           2                     2                     4
  ```

  For instance, 爱 looking at 猫: `[1, 2] · [1, 1] = 1 + 2 = 3`.

  **Step 2: scale.** Divide everything by √d\_k = √2 ≈ 1.414:

  ```
  我  [0.707, 0.000, 0.707]
  爱  [0.707, 1.414, 2.121]
  猫  [1.414, 1.414, 2.828]
  ```

  **Step 3: softmax.** Apply it to each row separately, so each row becomes weights summing to 1:

  ```
          looks at 我   looks at 爱   looks at 猫
  我         0.401         0.198         0.401
  爱         0.140         0.284         0.576
  猫         0.164         0.164         0.673
  ```

  **Step 4: weighted sum of V.** For 爱:

  ```
  0.140 × [2, 0] + 0.284 × [0, 1] + 0.576 × [2, 1]
  = [0.280 + 1.152,  0.284 + 0.576]
  = [1.432, 0.860]
  ```

  All three words:

  ```
  我 → [1.604, 0.599]
  爱 → [1.432, 0.860]
  猫 → [1.673, 0.836]
  ```

  Three vectors in, three vectors out, but each now carries information from the whole sentence. Compared with Level 2, **the skeleton is identical (score → softmax → weighted average)**, with two additions: the W\_Q, W\_K, W\_V projections at the start, and dividing the scores by √d\_k.

  ### Why divide by √d\_k?

  Level 0 mentioned that dot products grow with the size of the numbers. The specific problem here is that **dot products grow with dimension**.

  If every component of q and k is random with mean 0 and variance 1, then `q · k = q₁k₁ + q₂k₂ + … + q_d k_d` adds d terms, giving variance d and standard deviation √d. Real models often use 128 dims per head, so a typical dot product lands around ±11, not ±1.

  Large scores push softmax into saturation — the relative gaps stay the same, but the result changes completely:

  ```
  softmax([1,  2,  3])  = [0.090, 0.245,    0.665]    ← every position gets some weight
  softmax([10, 20, 30]) = [0.000, 0.000045, 0.99996]  ← almost all on one
  softmax([30, 60, 90]) = [0.0,   0.0,      1.0]      ← fully saturated
  ```

  Once saturated, the top entry is already 1 and the rest are 0, so nudging the parameters doesn't change the output and the gradient goes to nearly zero — the "won't train" problem from Level 0.

  **Dividing by √d\_k brings the standard deviation back to 1**, keeping scores in the range where softmax can learn, whatever the dimension. That's dividing by 8 for 64-dim heads and by about 11.3 for 128-dim heads.

  <Note title="Divide by √d_k, not by d_k">
    The goal is a **standard deviation** of 1. The variance is d\_k, so the standard deviation is √d\_k — hence √d\_k. That's the answer when someone asks "why the square root."
  </Note>

  ### Matrix form: how are all tokens computed at once?

  The walkthrough went word by word, but real computation handles every token together with matrices. The formula is the one line from the paper:

  ```
  Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q · Kᵀ / √d_k ) · V
  ```

  Shapes at each step (n tokens):

  ```
  X              [n, d_model]
  Q, K           [n, d_k]
  Q · Kᵀ         [n, n]        row i, column j = token i's score for token j (the 3×3 table above)
  softmax        [n, n]        applied per row
  × V            [n, d_v]      one new vector per token
  ```

  With a batch, add a leading dimension: the score table becomes `[batch, n, n]`.

  <Note title="Remember this n × n" type="tip">
    Every token scores every other token, so n tokens means n² scores. "Why is long context expensive" and "what does FlashAttention save" both start from this table; Level 8 works through it with real numbers.
  </Note>

  ### Why can self-attention run in parallel, and which Level 1 weakness does it fix?

  Look back at the computation: **computing 猫's result never waits for 我 or 爱 to finish.** Every token's Q, K, and V come out of a single matrix multiply, and all n × n dot products happen at once. Big matrix multiplies are exactly what GPUs do best.

  ```
  RNN:             h₁ → h₂ → h₃ → …   each step waits for the last
  Self-attention:  every position at once   one matrix multiply
  ```

  So **self-attention fixes weakness ② (no parallelism)**. It also eases "forgetting over long sentences": in an RNN the first word has to pass through n steps to affect the nth, while in self-attention any two words are just **one step** apart.

  <Note title="But it introduces a new problem" type="tip">
    Look closely at the computation: the scores depend only on the vectors' contents and **never use which position a word is in**. What happens if you reverse the sentence? Level 4 checks it with these same numbers and adds position information.
  </Note>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Three fixes that make self-attention usable

  The self-attention from Level 3 works in principle, but training a model with it as-is hits three gaps: **one set of weights can express only one kind of relationship**, **it has no idea of word order**, and **it can see positions it shouldn't**. This Level fills them one at a time.

  ### Why multi-head attention?

  In Level 3, each word got **one** set of weights. But a sentence holds many kinds of relationships at once.

  Take `it` in `"The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired."`:

  * coreference: `it` refers to `animal`
  * syntax: `it` is the subject of `was`
  * proximity: `it` sits right after `because`

  One set of weights can only average these, and the average expresses none of them clearly.

  **Multi-head attention runs h independent attentions at once.** Each one is called a head, has its own W\_Q, W\_K, W\_V, and can learn a different relationship; the results are then concatenated:

  ```
  head 1:  Q₁ K₁ V₁     → attention → output₁
  head 2:  Q₂ K₂ V₂     → attention → output₂
  …
  head h:  Q_h K_h V_h  → attention → output_h

  concatenate [output₁, output₂, …, output_h]  → multiply by an output matrix W_O  → final result
  ```

  **How are the dimensions divided?** Each head doesn't get the full width; d\_model is split evenly across h heads:

  ```
  original Transformer:  d_model = 512,   8 heads,  512 / 8   = 64 dims per head
  LLaMA 2 7B:            d_model = 4096,  32 heads, 4096 / 32 = 128 dims per head
  ```

  The shapes through one layer of LLaMA 2 7B:

  ```
  X                          [n, 4096]
  × W_Q, then split into 32  [32, n, 128]      128 dims per head
  attention in each head     [32, n, 128]
  concatenate back           [n, 4096]
  × W_O                      [n, 4096]
  ```

  **Total compute is about the same as a single 4096-dim head**: one big space is cut into 32 small ones computed in parallel, not multiplied by 32. W\_O mixes what the heads learned back into one vector.

  <Note title="“Each head learns one relationship” is intuition, not a guarantee" type="warning">
    Research does find heads that attend to the previous word or handle coreference, but most heads learn things that don't map to human-readable roles, and many can be pruned with little loss. "Multiple subspaces capture different kinds of dependencies" is fine in an interview; "head 3 handles grammar" is not.
  </Note>

  ### Why does self-attention need position information?

  Check with the numbers from Level 3. Reverse the sentence into 「猫 爱 我」, keep W\_Q, W\_K, W\_V the same, and recompute:

  ```
            output for 「我 爱 猫」    output for 「猫 爱 我」
  我          [1.604, 0.599]            [1.604, 0.599]
  爱          [1.432, 0.860]            [1.432, 0.860]
  猫          [1.673, 0.836]            [1.673, 0.836]
  ```

  **Every word's result is identical** — only the order they come out in changed. The scores depend only on the contents of q and k and never use position. To self-attention, 「我 爱 猫」 and 「猫 爱 我」 are the same set of vectors, so it can't tell who loves whom.

  An RNN reads in order and knows sequence for free; self-attention gave up reading in order to run in parallel, so **position has to be given to the model explicitly**.

  ### Why not just add the position index 1, 2, 3?

  The most obvious idea is to add each token's position number, but it has three problems:

  1. **The values blow up**: embedding values sit around ±1, while position 50,000 is 50,000; adding it drowns out the meaning entirely
  2. **Normalizing doesn't fix it**: with "position / length," the 5th word is 0.5 in a 10-word sentence but 0.05 in a 100-word one, so the model can't learn a stable meaning
  3. **Unseen lengths break**: if training never went past 1,024 and inference hits 2,000, that value is brand new to the model

  What's needed is a representation that's **bounded, different for every position, and regular across positions**.

  ### How is sinusoidal positional encoding computed?

  The original Transformer's scheme: sin and cos at different frequencies produce a vector P for each position, the same length as the embedding (d\_model), which is **added directly to the embedding**:

  ```
  P(pos, 2i)   = sin( pos / 10000^(2i / d) )
  P(pos, 2i+1) = cos( pos / 10000^(2i / d) )

  model input = X + P      shape still [n, d_model]
  ```

  By hand for the first three positions with d = 4 (dims 0–1 use frequency 1, dims 2–3 use 1/100):

  ```
  pos = 0   [sin 0,  cos 0,  sin 0,     cos 0   ]  = [0.000,  1.000, 0.000, 1.000]
  pos = 1   [sin 1,  cos 1,  sin 0.01,  cos 0.01]  = [0.841,  0.540, 0.010, 1.000]
  pos = 2   [sin 2,  cos 2,  sin 0.02,  cos 0.02]  = [0.909, -0.416, 0.020, 1.000]
  ```

  Think of it as **a clock with many hands**:

  * the early dimensions spin fast, like a second hand: neighboring positions differ a lot, which resolves nearby order
  * the later dimensions spin slowly, like an hour hand: they change only over long distances, which resolves roughly where something is far away
  * every value stays between -1 and 1, so meaning isn't drowned out, and every position gets a different combination of hands

  With positions added, 我 in 「我 爱 猫」 is "\[1, 0] + the vector for position 0," while 我 in 「猫 爱 我」 is "\[1, 0] + the vector for position 2." They're no longer the same, and self-attention can tell the orders apart.

  <Note title="Does adding position vectors to word vectors scramble the meaning?">
    Not in practice. d\_model is usually thousands of dimensions, which leaves plenty of room, and the Q, K, V projections learn during training to read both kinds of information out of the combined "meaning + position" vector. It's like music with left and right channels mixed together — you can still hear both the melody and where each sound comes from.
  </Note>

  ### What is learned positional encoding?

  The more direct alternative: **give positions their own learnable table, just like the vocabulary**, trained along with everything else.

  That's what GPT-2 does: a `[1024, 768]` position table with 786,432 parameters. Token pos takes row pos and adds it to its embedding.

  It's flexible — the model decides how to represent position — but **it has a hard ceiling**: the table has 1,024 rows, so position 1,025 has no vector at all. That's one reason GPT-2's context is capped at 1,024. Today's LLMs use RoPE, a different approach covered in Level 7.

  ### What does the padding mask do?

  Level 0 covered this: sentences in a batch differ in length, so short ones get padded with `<pad>`. But `<pad>` means nothing, and real words shouldn't attend to it.

  **The fix: before softmax, set the score for every `<pad>` position to negative infinity (-∞).** Since `e^(-∞) = 0`, that position gets exactly zero weight after softmax.

  Example: 「我 爱」 padded with one `<pad>`, where 我's row of scaled scores is `[0.707, 0.000, some number]`:

  ```
  no mask:    softmax([0.707, 0.000, some number])   → <pad> takes some of the weight
  with mask:  softmax([0.707, 0.000, -∞])            → [0.670, 0.330, 0.000]
  ```

  ### What does the causal mask do?

  Recall Level 1: the decoder is **autoregressive** and writes one word at a time. To train a decoder quickly, the whole target "I love cats" goes in **at once**, and every position learns "predict the next word" simultaneously:

  ```
  position 1 sees I          → should predict love
  position 2 sees I love     → should predict cats
  ```

  Here's the catch: by default, self-attention lets every word see the whole sentence. If position 1 could see "love" right after it, it would just copy the answer and learn nothing. And at inference the later words don't exist yet, so training wouldn't match inference.

  **The causal mask says: position i can look only at positions 1 through i, never ahead.** It's implemented just like the padding mask, by setting the scores for future positions to -∞.

  Check it with 「我 爱 猫」 from Level 3, comparing weights before and after:

  ```
               no mask                            with causal mask
            at 我   at 爱   at 猫               at 我   at 爱   at 猫
  我        0.401   0.198   0.401               1.000   0       0
  爱        0.140   0.284   0.576               0.330   0.670   0
  猫        0.164   0.164   0.673               0.164   0.164   0.673
  ```

  The outputs change too: 我 becomes `[2.000, 0.000]` (it can only see itself), 爱 becomes `[0.660, 0.670]`, and 猫, already last, is unaffected.

  The weight matrix is now **lower-triangular**. One matrix operation lets every position compute at once while each looks only at the past — the key reason Transformer training parallelizes and RNN training doesn't.

  <Note title="Padding mask vs. causal mask">
    Both use -∞, but they block different things: **the padding mask blocks meaningless filler; the causal mask blocks a future that shouldn't be visible yet.** Decoder training often uses both. An encoder needs only the padding mask, because every word reading the source should see the whole sentence.
  </Note>

  <Note title="The causal mask is what makes the KV cache possible" type="tip">
    Because word i never sees anything after it, its K and V **never change** once computed, no matter how many words follow — so they can be cached and reused. That's the KV cache in Level 8.
  </Note>
