title: Reranking
description: Top 50 → Cross Encoder / Reranker → Top 5。为什么分两阶段。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Be able to explain the compute budget of the recall stage versus the precision stage.

  ## Must know

  Retrieval is cheap and coarse; reranking is expensive and precise.

  ## Mechanism
</Locale>

```
Top 50 retrieved
        ↓
Cross Encoder / Reranker
        ↓
Top 5
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Re-sorting a small set of candidates with a stronger model, usually a cross-encoder.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  A bi-encoder encodes the query and documents separately, which is what lets document vectors be precomputed. A cross-encoder encodes them together — higher quality, but impossible to run across the whole corpus.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Rerank depth and candidate-set size directly drive latency. Without a reranker, invest in better hybrid search and metadata. With one, make sure it shows up in your traces.

  ## Interview questions

  1. Why reranking?
  2. Why are retrieval and reranking split into two stages?
  3. What happens if you go from Top 50 to Top 200?
  4. When is reranking not worth it?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: Sparse Retrieval
description: BM25、倒排索引、keyword search。和语义检索为什么互补。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  For proper nouns, error codes, and IDs, keyword search usually wins.

  ## Must know

  * BM25
  * inverted index
  * keyword search

  ## Mechanism

  ```
  term → posting list → BM25 score
  same meaning, different wording        → dense retrieval wins
  exact wording that embeddings blur out → BM25 wins
  ```

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Retrieval based on term statistics. BM25 is the most common sparse scoring function.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  An inverted index lists the documents each term appears in. BM25 penalizes very long documents and very common terms.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  It complements dense retrieval: one catches paraphrases, the other catches exact matches. That's the case for hybrid search — not "BM25 is outdated."

  ## Interview questions

  1. What does BM25 penalize, and what does it reward?
  2. Why do semantic search and keyword search complement each other?
  3. Which queries shouldn't rely on vector search alone?
  4. How do you keep inverted-index updates in sync with vector-index updates?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: Vector Search
description: ANN、HNSW、IVF、PQ、vector DB、metadata filtering。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  You must be able to answer: why can't you brute-force search every embedding?

  ## Must know

  * ANN
  * HNSW
  * IVF
  * PQ
  * vector DB
  * metadata filtering

  ## Mechanism

  ```
  exact kNN  →  O(N·d)  exact, but doesn't scale
  ANN        →  approximate nearest neighbors; trade a little recall for latency
  ```

  ## Three-level answers

  ### Level 1 — Definition

  Finding nearest neighbors among high-dimensional vectors. Production systems use approximate algorithms, not a full scan.

  ### Level 2 — Mechanism

  HNSW is a graph index; IVF clusters first and only scans some buckets per query; PQ compresses vectors to save memory. Whether metadata filtering runs before or after the vector search changes recall.

  ### Level 3 — Engineering

  Past a million or so vectors, brute force doesn't pay off in latency or CPU/GPU cost. Tuning HNSW's ef or IVF's nprobe moves you along a recall–latency curve; it isn't an on/off switch.

  ## Interview questions

  1. Why can't you just brute-force search every embedding?
  2. How do you choose between HNSW and IVF?
  3. How does PQ affect retrieval quality?
  4. Do you filter before retrieval or after?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

*

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: L2 · Meeting Summarization
description: 长音频 / 纪要：ASR、说话人、长上下文、异步。
content:

  It has to be asynchronous. Long transcripts need chunking with map-reduce, or a long window plus compression. Action items should come out as structured output.

audio → ASR + diarization → transcript store
      → chunk summarize → reduce → actions/JSON
